source: cross-examiner verdicts from the research fleets (one agent per contested claim, both lenses)

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: India (SIPRI country series) had a military burden of 2.3% of GDP in calendar year 2024, the median of the top 15 spenders, and ranked 5th in dollars. Every figure comes from the same SIPRI April 2025 release, so there is no window mismatch. The 'from: 2024' field is correct. The PRS source is out of window. It cites SIPRI 2023 data (India 4th, $84 bn, 2.4%) and the MoD budget-to-GDP ratio for 2025-26 (1.9%), not 2024.
verdicts.identityTest: The subject 'min:ministry-of-defence' is a loose fit. SIPRI's India figure is a national total that includes paramilitary forces: PRS says 'This includes spending on paramilitary forces', and SIPRI's methodology is the same. So the 2.3% is not the MoD budget. PRS puts the MoD's own figure at 'India is estimated to spend 1.9% of its GDP on defence' (2025-26). The peer set is exactly SIPRI Table 1, ranks 1-15. No entity is mismatched.
verdicts.baseRate: SIPRI 2024 Table 1, ranks 1-15, burden sorted: 1.4 (Japan), 1.6 (Italy), 1.7 (China), 1.9 (Germany), 1.9 (Australia), 2.1 (France), 2.3 (India), 2.3 (UK), 2.6 (South Korea), 3.4 (USA), 4.2 (Poland), 7.1 (Russia), 7.3 (Saudi Arabia), 8.8 (Israel), 34 (Ukraine). The 8th of 15 is 2.3, so the median is correct. India is tied with the UK at that value. Seven of the other fourteen spend a larger share and six a smaller one; the record text is correct. The world burden is 2.5%. By construction, being at the median does not single India out from its peers. That is the claim's point, and it alleges nothing.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was asked for. The claim is a neutral benchmark that alleges nothing, so no party has anything to respond to.
verdicts.innocentReading: India spends close to the peer-group norm. The 2.3% includes paramilitary spending, so it overstates the MoD-only burden, which PRS puts at about 1.9% for 2025-26. The Standing Committee's 3% figure is a domestic target, not a peer norm. These benign readings are already the claim's own reading. Nothing in it implies under- or over-spending or wrongdoing.
verdicts.reason: The SIPRI fact sheet, which I opened, confirms every number. Table 1 lists 'India 86.1 ... 2.3', rank 5. The text says 'India, the fifth biggest military spender in the world in 2024, increased its spending to $86.1 billion'. The world burden is 2.5%. Recomputing the median of the 15 burden figures gives 2.3. The claim does not chain facts into an implication. It is a pure comparison, so analytic is the right tier. The weak point is the second source: PRS does not support the 2024 figures. It uses 2023 SIPRI data (India 4th, 2.4%) and a different measure (MoD budget, 1.9% of GDP). It supports only the context about the Standing Committee's 3% figure.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Label the PRS source as context only: '2023 SIPRI comparison and Standing Committee 3% recommendation; PRS gives 1.9% MoD budget/GDP for 2025-26, a different measure'. Alternatively, drop it from the srcs of the 2.3%/fifth claim. (2) Add to d: 'SIPRI's India figure includes paramilitary forces; MoD-budget-only burden is lower (PRS: 1.9% in 2025-26).' (3) Add to d or lab: 'tied with the UK at 2.3%'. (4) Optionally re-point s from min:ministry-of-defence to a national 'India (SIPRI)' node, or note that the SIPRI total goes beyond the MoD. (5) The citation 'table 1 and p. 5' is fine. The 'fifth biggest' sentence is in the India paragraph on p. 4-5.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Ministry of Defence's 2025-26 BE allocates about 24% to pensions and about 50% to pay plus pensions (PRS, 4 Feb 2025), and in 2022-23 P&A plus pension were 79% of MoD revenue expenditure (ORF Issue Brief 567, 16 Aug 2023). Each figure sits in the right fiscal year in its own source. One caveat: ORF's 2022-23 figure is a budget estimate, not actuals. ORF says "In 2022-23, P&A and Pension will add up to INR 287,040 crore, or 79 percent of the MoD's total revenue expenditure", and its Figure 1 note reads "Figures for 2021-22 and 2022-23 are revised and budget estimates". The claim should label 2022-23 as BE. Edge from:'2025' is fine for the PRS half. The ORF half dates from 2023.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the Ministry of Defence, the same body both sources name. One wording problem: Rs 6,81,210 crore is the MoD's total allocation across all its demands (MoD Civil, Defence Services Revenue, Capital Outlay, Defence Pensions), not a single "defence demand". PRS says: "the central government has allocated Rs 6,81,210 crore for the Ministry of Defence". PRS also notes that "Salaries include pay and allowances of the armed forces, auxiliary forces, civilians, research and development, and salary expenditure of the civil estimates." So "pay" includes civilians and R&D staff, not only the armed forces. PRS adds that salaries "could be an underestimate as detailed breakup for revenue expenditure on Rashtriya Rifles, National Cadet Corps, and the Agnipath cadre is not available."
verdicts.baseRate: Not discriminating, and the claim makes no accusation. A large personnel and pension share is structural for the MoD under every government. From ORF's own numbers, pensions were about 18% of MoD spending in 2013-14 under UPA-II (Rs 45,500 crore). PRS reports 24% in 2025-26 under the NDA. The rise is put down to OROP and the 7th CPC. The same lens applied to the UPA-II years gives the same descriptive reading: a high committed share. No rival, state or vendor control applies, because this is a budget-composition statistic, not conduct.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was sought. The claim imputes no conduct to any party, so no response is owed. The figures are the government's own budget numbers as transcribed by PRS.
verdicts.innocentReading: Pensions are deferred pay owed under service contracts. Their share rose because of policy choices about people: OROP (2015) and the 7th CPC (2016). It does not show waste. PRS also notes that the 2025-26 pension line is inflated by a one-off Rs 8,000 crore recovery from a deposit account. One error in the record's innocentReading: it says "about 26.8 lakh pensioners", but ORF gives 32,94,181 pensioners as of 1 April 2021 (26,79,645 military veterans or dependents plus 6,14,536 defence civilians). The pension line covers both groups.
verdicts.reason: Every number checks out against the sources, which I opened and quoted. In the PRS PDF, Table 2 has Pension 1,60,795, Salaries 1,77,923 and Total 6,81,210 for 2025-26 BE. The text says "In 2025-26, 24% of the total defence budget is estimated to be spent on pension" and "Salaries and pension account for 50% of the estimated spending on defence in 2025-26." The ORF brief says "79 percent of the MoD's total revenue expenditure" for 2022-23, and gives pension growth of 163% against 107% for MoD overall between 2013-14 and 2022-23. My arithmetic: 23.6% and 49.7%. The claim does not combine facts to imply wrongdoing, names no individual and contains no operational detail. Analytic is a conservative tier. Because both outlets state these exact percentages themselves, 'reported' would also be defensible. The fixes needed are wording only: say BE, say "MoD total allocation", and correct the pensioner count.
verdicts.corrections: 1. text/lab: replace "the 2025-26 defence demand" with "the MoD's total 2025-26 BE allocation (Rs 6,81,210 crore, all demands)". 2. text/d: change "79% of revenue expenditure 2022-23" to "79% of MoD revenue expenditure, 2022-23 BE (ORF, Aug 2023)". 3. d: add PRS's caveats that "salaries" includes civilians, R&D and civil estimates but leaves out Rashtriya Rifles, NCC and the Agnipath cadre, and that the 2025-26 pension line includes a Rs 8,000 crore deposit-account recovery. 4. innocentReading: change "about 26.8 lakh pensioners" to "about 32.9 lakh pensioners (26.8 lakh military veterans or dependents plus 6.1 lakh defence civilians, as of 1 Apr 2021, per ORF)". 5. Optional: the tier could be raised to 'reported' with note 'reported: PRS transcription of Union Budget 2025-26', because the percentages are stated verbatim by PRS and ORF, not computed by us. Keeping 'analytic' is acceptable.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: PRS Legislative Research reported, on 4 Feb 2025, that the Ministry of Defence is 13% of central expenditure in 2025-26 BE, down from 17% in 2014-15, and that defence is 1.9% of GDP against the Standing Committee on Defence's 2018 recommendation of about 3%. The PDF is dated February 4, 2025, which matches the record's from=2025-02. The 2025-26 figures are Budget Estimates. The 17% for 2014-15 comes from PRS's time series, which mixes actuals and BE/RE, so the comparison is actual against BE. PRS states this mix in its own note ("BE is budget estimate and RE is revised estimate"). Neither the dates nor the ministers involved have an overlap problem, because the claim is purely descriptive.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is correct: the Ministry of Defence demand as a whole, Rs 6,81,210 crore including pensions and civil. It is not the narrower "Defence Services" figure. Quoted from p.1: "In 2025-26, the Ministry has been allocated Rs 6,81,210 crore ... The allocation towards the Ministry is the largest across all ministries and accounts for 13% of the total expenditure of the central government." And: "In 2014-15, the Centre spent 17% of its total budget on defence which reduced to 13% as per the budget estimates of 2025-26. Between 2013-14 and 2025-26, compared to an annual increase of 9% in defence spending, total central government expenditure increased at an annual rate of 10%." And: "The Standing Committee on Defence (2018) had recommended that the Ministry of Defence should be allocated a fixed budget of about 3% of GDP ... In 2025-26, India is estimated to spend 1.9% of its GDP on defence." Rough cross-check: 6.81 lakh crore against Budget at a Glance total expenditure of about 50.65 lakh crore gives about 13.4%. Against nominal GDP BE of about 357 lakh crore it gives about 1.9%. Every number, the fiscal year, the stage and the actor match the source.
verdicts.baseRate: The figures are not discriminating, and the claim alleges no wrongdoing. No Indian government since the early 1990s has met the 3%-of-GDP level. PRS's own chart shows a steady decline from 2013-14 onward. The UPA-II control (FY2009-14) had defence also falling as a share of GDP and of central spending, and also below 3%. Defence's share shrinking as the overall budget grows faster is the normal pattern for India. The 2014-15 starting year happens to be the first NDA budget. That could be read as a partisan baseline, so a UPA-II comparison should sit next to it.
verdicts.denialFound: The Ministry of Defence's position appears inside the same PRS PDF (p.2), citing the Standing Committee report: "According to the Ministry of Defence, spending 3% of India's GDP on the defence sector will lead to much higher allocations which the defence services may not be able to absorb." This is the Ministry's own documented response on the 3% benchmark. No denial of the share figures exists, and none is needed because they are arithmetic from budget documents.
verdicts.innocentReading: The defence budget is growing in absolute terms (9% a year) while total central spending grows faster (10% a year), so defence's share falls without any cut. The Ministry itself says the services could not absorb 3% of GDP. The GDP ratio counts MoD pensions; leaving pensions out lowers it by about 0.5 percentage points. It also excludes MHA's paramilitary forces (CAPFs).
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the claim. The PRS PDF states each figure word for word: 13% in 2025-26 BE, 17% in 2014-15, 1.9% of GDP, and the Standing Committee on Defence (2018) recommendation of about 3%. The figures also roughly reproduce from Budget at a Glance totals. "Reported" is the right tier: PRS is one credible outlet doing analysis from published documents. It would move to "documented" once the ratios are rebuilt directly from indiabudget.gov.in. The claim is fair only if three things are added: that 2025-26 is BE, that the committee report is from 2018, and the Ministry's absorption-capacity response that PRS itself quotes.
verdicts.corrections:
1. text: change to "Defence 13% of Union expenditure in 2025-26 BE (17% in 2014-15); 1.9% of GDP vs Standing Committee on Defence (2018) recommendation of about 3% (PRS)."
2. d: add "MoD stated 3% of GDP would produce allocations the services may not be able to absorb (PRS p.2, citing the Standing Committee report)." Also add that the 1.9% includes pensions; excluding them gives about 1.4-1.5%.
3. Add a symmetryCheck noting the decline began before 2014. Report the UPA-II FY2009-14 share and GDP ratio from the same Budget documents, so the 2014-15 baseline is not read as partisan.
4. upgradeIf: keep as is. When the union-defence domain reproduces 6,81,210 / total expenditure and / nominal GDP from Budget at a Glance 2025-26, raise to documented.
5. Leave tier=reported and pred=analytic as they are.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: PRS Legislative Research reported, in its Feb 2025 DFG analysis, that MHA's police allocation in the 2025-26 Budget Estimate was Rs 1,60,391 crore, 69% of the ministry total. The figure is a BE for FY 2025-26. The record's "from: 2025-02" matches the date the PRS note was published. Nothing about tenure or ownership needs to overlap, because the actor is the Union Budget. One caveat: the 2025-26 Revised Estimates were published in the Feb 2026 Union Budget, so this BE figure may since have been revised. The claim names the stage as BE, so it is not wrong, but it is not the latest figure.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is right. The PDF is "Demand for Grants 2025-26 Analysis — Home Affairs" (PRS, Niranjana S Menon). Table 1 gives "Police 1,24,715 / 1,46,833 / 1,60,391 / 9%" and "Total ... 2,33,211 / 6%". The "85%" figure refers to the police head, not the whole MHA, and the claim's wording "85% of it" reads it the same way.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable. This is a descriptive budget-share figure with an 'analytic' predicate. It implies no wrongdoing and does not single out any actor, so there is no discriminating property to test against a base rate. Symmetry check: the same arithmetic run on a UPA-II-era MHA DFG would give a similar result, with CAPFs dominating the police head. The claim does not depend on which government is in power.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was sought. The claim alleges nothing, so no party has anything to deny.
verdicts.innocentReading: The Union's police demand pays for forces the Union itself runs: CAPFs, Delhi Police, J&K Police after 2019, and border infrastructure. State police are paid for from state budgets and are not in this number. The 85% concentration is therefore structural and does not reflect a policy choice. The record already carries this reading.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the claim. Every number matches the source PDF text. Quotes: "In 2025-26, Rs 1,60,391 crore has been budgeted for police expenditure. A majority of this expenditure (85% of total allocation) is towards the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF), the Delhi and J&K police, and border infrastructure." Table 1 is headed "69% of the Ministry's expenditure in 2025-26 will be towards police". "Rs 21,258 crore has been allocated to Delhi police and J&K police together ... 13% of the total allocation towards police." The arithmetic checks out against the BE column of Table 2: CAPF 1,09,037 + Delhi Police 11,932 + J&K Police 9,326 + Border Infrastructure 5,597 = 1,35,892, which is 84.7% of 1,60,391. 11,932 + 9,326 = 21,258. 1,60,391 / 2,33,211 = 68.8%. The claim does not combine separate facts to suggest something none of them says. The tier is 'reported' because it rests on a single credible secondary analysis built from published Budget documents. 'Documented' would be justified once the figure is reproduced from the Union Budget Expenditure Profile or from the MHA demand itself.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Optionally make "85%" exact in field d: "CAPF 1,09,037 + Delhi Police 11,932 + J&K Police 9,326 + Border Infrastructure 5,597 = 1,35,892 crore (84.7% of police, BE)". 2. Note in d that "border infrastructure" is the PRS Table 2 line 'Border Infrastructure' (5,597), which is separate from 'Police Infrastructure' (4,379). 3. Add the PRS HTML page as a second source link if one exists. To meet the upgradeIf condition, reproduce the figures from the Union Budget 2025-26 MHA police demand (indiabudget.gov.in, sbe48 or the equivalent demand number), not from 'Demand 48' as the record assumes; check the demand number. 4. Add a note that the 2025-26 RE (Union Budget, Feb 2026) may supersede the BE figure; record it in 'supersededBy' if the RE differs materially. No change to the tier.

verdicts.dateTest: As written: "Ministry of Defence denied c006 from 2019-03." The two parts of the claim come from different dates. (1) The privilege argument was made by the Attorney General for the Union in the review proceedings (March 2019) and rejected on 2019-04-10. So 2019-03 fits that part. (2) The price defence predates c006 by months. Jaitley's 9%/20% statement and M.J. Akbar's Times of India op-ed (₹538 to ₹737 crore, ₹670 crore, 9%, 20%) are from the 2018 controversy. Ravi Shankar Prasad's €100.85m vs €91.75m comparison was made in the July 2018 Macron row (Wikipedia places it just after the no-confidence debate of 20 July 2018). Modi's "liars" remark was on 2018-12-16. None of these statements can be a response to a 2019-04-10 ruling. The price material also does not contradict c006 at all, since c006 is only about whether the documents are admissible. The `contra` edge holds only for the privilege part.
verdicts.identityTest: This test fails. The record says "the then Defence Minister said the 2007 bid (₹526 crore per aircraft, escalating to ₹737 crore by 2015) and the 2016 IGA basic price (~₹670 crore) were not comparable and the IGA saved about 20%". Wikipedia gives the ₹737 crore, 9% and 20% figures to two other people. First, M.J. Akbar, Minister of State for External Affairs, in an op-ed: "Dassault's bid had been accepted at ₹538 crore along with a price escalation formula that would have increased the price to ₹737 crore in 2015... IGA price of ₹670 crore for each basic aircraft represented a 9% decrease... the IGA price was 20% lower". Second, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley: "the basic aircraft was 9% cheaper and the overall agreement was 20% cheaper". The Defence Minister, Sitharaman, said only that "the prices could not be compared" and that "the figure of ₹526 crore quoted by Congress represented the cost of basic aircraft". The ~₹670 crore figure came from MoS Defence Subhash Bhamre in Parliament. The record also merges ₹526 crore (Congress's figure) with Akbar's ₹538 crore base. The subject `min:ministry-of-defence` is wrong for most of the content. The privilege argument was made by the Attorney General for the Union of India (SC order: "The learned Attorney General contends that ... three documents unauthorizedly removed from the office of the Ministry of Defence"). The price defence came from the Finance Minister, the Law Minister, the MoS External Affairs and the PM.
verdicts.baseRate: The test barely applies: this is a single case, and the claim records a respondent's position. On symmetry, governments of both alliances claim secrecy over defence pricing. Wikipedia records Jaitley citing 15 UPA-era refusals to disclose arms expenditure, and the 2008 security agreement was signed by UPA minister A.K. Antony. For Bofors, the control case, the same lens would record the Rajiv Gandhi government's denials as contra in the same way. Recording the government's case is evenhanded and should stay.
verdicts.denialFound: This record is itself the government's response. Contrary material exists. (a) The SC order of 2019-04-10 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/126750916/) rejected the privilege argument, saying s.123 covers "unpublished public records", while "the three documents have been published in different editions of 'The Hindu'". (b) The CAG report of February 2019 is reported to have found the IGA about 2.86% cheaper, not 9–20%. literature.json line ~1010 records this as not opened because cag.gov.in was unreachable. (c) Congress (Surjewala, Rahul Gandhi) disputes the comparison (Wikipedia).
verdicts.innocentReading: The government's case is that a basic-aircraft price cannot be compared with a fully loaded, India-specific package. On that view, the 2007 bid with its 3.9% escalation is the right baseline, and on that basis the IGA came out cheaper. This reading is internally coherent and is the defence the record should carry. The record's errors are attribution errors, not a slant.
verdicts.reason: The headline survives: the privilege claim was rejected by the SC, and a 9–20% saving was claimed. The SC order confirms the privilege part verbatim, and Wikipedia confirms the 9%/20% figures. But the `d` field puts figures in the mouth of "the then Defence Minister" when the source gives them to M.J. Akbar and Arun Jaitley. It also uses ₹526 crore where that chain started at ₹538 crore. And the subject is MoD for statements made by other ministers and the AG. Putting a statement in the mouth of an office-holder who did not make it fails the identity test. The 2019-03 date and the `contra` target also fit only the privilege part. Treat the record as refuted until it is corrected; once corrected it stands at `reported`.
verdicts.corrections: 1) d: replace "the then Defence Minister said the 2007 bid (₹526 crore ... ₹737 crore by 2015) ... saved about 20%" with: "Defence Minister Sitharaman said the prices were not comparable and that Congress's ₹526 crore was the basic-aircraft cost. MoS Defence Bhamre told Parliament the IGA cost was ~₹670 crore per aircraft. Finance Minister Jaitley said the basic aircraft was 9% cheaper and the package 20% cheaper. MoS External Affairs M.J. Akbar wrote that the bid accepted at ₹538 crore would have escalated to ₹737 crore by 2015." 2) s: the privilege argument should be `Union of India / Attorney General`. Best fix is to split into two records: c007a (privilege, subject Union/AG, from 2019-03, contra c006, with the SC order as source) and c007b (price defence, 2018, contra to the Congress overpricing narrative, not to c006). 3) from: 2019-03 holds only for the privilege part; the price statements belong to the 2018 controversy, with Modi's remark on 2018-12-16. 4) Add to d: "CAG (Feb 2019) reported as 2.86% cheaper — not opened". 5) text: "like-for-like saving 9–20% claimed" should read "9% (basic aircraft) to 20% (package) claimed by ministers Jaitley/Akbar/Prasad".

verdicts.dateTest: I tested three dated parts. (1) Swiss documents: the Delhi HC judgment (indiankanoon 561739) says "the second set of documents was received in January 1997 from the Swiss authority". It also lists Swiss tranches received in December 1990, December 1999, 2 June 2000 and 4 October 2000. The McIntyre/Hinduja payments were "revealed" by the December 1999 set, not the 1997 set. So "1997" is one tranche among several, and Wikipedia's "some 500 documents" figure carries no citation. (2) Closure: Wikipedia says that on 4 March 2011 a Delhi court allowed CBI to close the case against Quattrocchi (citing ET, 5 March 2011, and TOI). That matches the claim. (3) SC dismissal: Hindustan Times (7 August 2026) says "A Supreme Court bench on Thursday dismissed the last existing appeal against the 2005 Delhi high court judgment". 6 August 2026 was a Thursday, and DNA and Republic (7 August 2026) agree. The dates hold.
verdicts.identityTest: The claim fails on who filed the plea. The record's d-field says "CBI's later attempts to revive ended with the Supreme Court dismissing the final plea on 2026-08-06". HT says the dismissed appeal was filed by "advocate Ajay K Agrawal, who had challenged the high court verdict as a private appellant". It adds that the SC "had already dismissed the Central Bureau of Investigation's appeal against the same high court judgment in November 2018 ... delay of 4,522 days". The 2026 order is therefore not CBI's. It is also about the 2005 Delhi HC discharge of the Hindujas and AB Bofors, not the 2011 Quattrocchi closure. The killIf condition ("2026 order concerns a different petition") is not triggered, because this is the last surviving plea. But the claim and its framing must not attribute it to CBI. The other names match the sources: Italian agent = Ottavio Quattrocchi / AE Services; agents = Svenska/Win Chadha, AE Services/Quattrocchi, McIntyre/Moresco (Hindujas).
verdicts.baseRate: Not a cohort property, so a base-rate test does not apply. This is a single-case enforcement chronology. The SPEC symmetry control is Rafale. The SC dismissed the Rafale petitions (Dec 2018) and the review petitions (Nov 2019), CBI never registered an FIR, and a French PNF judicial inquiry opened in 2021. The Rafale record should carry identical fields: agency action, closure, final SC disposal, and whether recipient-side evidence exists. Bofors has a documented agent-payment trail but no recipient trail. Rafale has neither in an Indian court record.
verdicts.denialFound: The exculpatory record is in the cited source itself. Delhi HC, 4 February 2004 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/561739/): the ASG for CBI conceded that, as to bribe receipt by public servants, "till date there was none". The court held the late PM "is entitled to be seen as innocent". BBC, 25 April 2012 (cited on Wikipedia): Swedish investigator Sten Lindstrom said there was "No evidence Rajiv Gandhi took bribe". The JPC report (1988) found no evidence that the payments violated Indian law. I found no separate 2026 statement from the Hindujas or Bofors, and none appears to have been sought. Both Hinduja respondents who died (Srichand and Gopichand) are deceased.
verdicts.innocentReading: Bofors paid commissions to agents. That breached its assurance to the Government of India that it used no middlemen, and the HC judgment documents those payments. But a payment to an agent is not a bribe to a public servant. In 2004 the prosecution conceded it had no evidence of receipt by officials. The 2011 and 2026 disposals reflect evidentiary failure, deaths, and a 4,522-day CBI delay rather than a finding of either guilt or innocence. The claim's wording "recipient side never established" already states this reading correctly.
verdicts.reason: The core conjunction survives. Payments to agents are confirmed by a primary court record: the Delhi HC says CBI "succeeded in tracing the Swiss accounts of 'Commission Agents' employed by M/s A.B. Bofors wherein illegal payments received by them from Bofors as commission were deposited". The same judgment records the ASG's concession that there was no evidence of public servants receiving bribes. The 4 March 2011 Quattrocchi closure and the 6 August 2026 SC dismissal are reported by multiple outlets (HT, DNA, Republic, NewsX). Two errors need fixing. First, the d-field attributes the 2026 plea to CBI, but it was the private appellant Ajay K Agrawal's appeal; CBI's own appeal died in November 2018 on delay. Second, "Swiss documents (1997)" understates the timeline: the documents came in tranches from 1990 to 2000, and the 1997 tranche is not shown to be the one that "establishes" the payments. As sourced, the record rests on Wikipedia for 2011 and 2026, so it stays at reported. It becomes documented once the HT and DNA URLs (or the SC order itself) are added; the agent-payment and no-recipient elements already rest on a court order.
verdicts.corrections: 1. d-field: replace "CBI's later attempts to revive ended with the Supreme Court dismissing the final plea on 2026-08-06" with "The SC dismissed CBI's own appeal against the 2005 HC discharge in November 2018 for a 4,522-day delay. The last surviving appeal, by private appellant Ajay K Agrawal, was dismissed on 2026-08-06 (Pardiwala and Vinod Chandran JJ)." 2. Text: change "Swiss documents (1997)" to "Swiss documents received in tranches 1990–2000 (incl. Jan 1997)". Drop "about 500" or cite it. 3. Make clear that the 2026 order concerned the 2005 HC quashing for the Hindujas and AB Bofors, not the 2011 Quattrocchi closure. 4. srcs: add https://www.hindustantimes.com/ht-explainers/supreme-court-draws-the-curtain-on-bofors-scandal-case-explained-rajiv-gandhi-1999-kargil-war-bofors-howitzers-101786086628284-amp.html and https://www.dnaindia.com/india/report-bofors-chapter-closed-as-supreme-court-rejects-appeal-against-delhi-hc-relief-to-hinduja-brothers-3217972. Also add the ET piece of 5 March 2011 for the closure, so the record does not rest on Wikipedia. With these added, upgrade to documented. 5. Pair this record with force:case-rafale using identical fields, per the SPEC control.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MoD (UPA-II, Defence Minister A.K. Antony) terminated the 8 Feb 2010 AWIL contract on 2014-01-01 and had recovered ₹2,068 crore by June 2014. Both the actor's tenure and the contract window overlap the action. The MoD statement dated 1 January 2014 is reported by CNBC and Business Standard on 2014-01-01. Wikipedia says "in January 2014", and its cited NIE article is dated 2014/01/01. Wikipedia gives the June 2014 total recovery date: "in June 2014, the Indian government encashed ₹18.18 billion, taking the total amount recovered so far to ₹20.68 billion." The date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the Ministry of Defence, Government of India. The counterparty is AgustaWestland International Ltd (AWIL), a Finmeccanica subsidiary. The contract is the one signed 8 Feb 2010 for 12 AW101 VVIP helicopters, about €556–560m or ₹3,600 crore. The source names this same entity and contract. Units are correct: ₹20.68 billion = ₹2,068 crore, made up of ₹250 crore encashed in India in January 2014 plus ₹1,818 crore from Italian bank guarantees in June 2014.
verdicts.baseRate: This does not apply in a discriminating sense. The edge records a single enforcement act, not a shared property. The ₹2,068 crore is gross encashment, not net loss recovery: India paid about ₹1,620 crore (45%) and kept three aircraft, and Agusta disputes €106m of it.

He landed on the night of 4 December. The record's 2018-12-04 is defensible, but the d field should note the 4/5 Dec ambiguity. The "Indian trial pending" part still holds as of 2026-10-04. The Delhi HC rejected Michel's plea for release on 2026-04-08 (supremetoday.ai). In May 2026 the SC asked the Centre to respond to his plea against continued detention, listed for July 2026 (barandbench.com). I found no verdict in an Indian court. Tyagi's tenure as IAF chief was 2004–07. The 2003 change to the helicopter specifications came before his tenure, under the NSA/PMO (Tyagi's defence). That does not affect the enforcement edge.

So the identical-fields comparison cannot be run yet. That is a gap in the control, not a defect in this claim. A slow, unresolved Indian trial (more than 12 years since the FIR, no verdict) is the norm for high-profile CBI corruption cases: Bofors never reached trial, and the Tatra outcome is not recorded. He says the decision to change the specifications was taken by a group of senior officials before his tenure, and his counsel argued in court that "CBI in the last four years has never been able to establish any evidence against ex-air chief regarding receipt of any bribe" (https://www.india.com/news/india/sp-tyagi-granted-bail-in-agustawestland-chopper-scam-case-1724022/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashindra_Pal_Tyagi). verdicts.innocentReading: An FIR and arrests are steps in an investigation, not findings of guilt. Twelve years with no Indian verdict fits ordinary CBI and trial-court delay, plus extradition-specialty litigation, as well as it fits a weak case. The Italian acquittals were for insufficient evidence. They do not prove the absence of a bribe, and they do not prove a bribe either. The claim as worded does not overreach toward guilt.
verdicts.reason: I opened the single cited source (the raw text of the Wikipedia article). It states every element of the claim. The FIR line reads: "registered an FIR on 13 March 2013. The FIR named 13 persons ... The FIR also named four companies". It reports the CBI arrests of 9 December 2016, Michel's extradition in December 2018, the Milan acquittal of 8 January 2018 "upheld by the Supreme Court of Cassazione on 22 May 2019", and Michel remaining "an accused in the separate CBI corruption case" in December 2025. 2026 reporting (Delhi HC 2026-04-08, SC hearings May–July 2026) confirms there is still no Indian verdict. One sentence is incomplete: "Italian courts ended in acquittal" leaves out that in August 2014 AgustaWestland SpA and AgustaWestland Ltd took a plea bargain (patteggiamento) in Busto Arsizio. A patteggiamento is not a finding of guilt, but omitting it makes the claim read more exculpatory than the Italian record is. That calls for a correction, not a kill. So 2022-08-25 is the date the findings were disclosed in court, not the date the report was written or filed. Raveendran supervised the committee.
verdicts.baseRate: Does not apply. This is a single factual report of a court-appointed inquiry's findings, not a claim about how common a property is. No comparison set is implied. On symmetry: the claim says nothing about wrongdoing, and it states that Pegasus was not conclusively shown.

verdicts.innocentReading: Finding malware on 5 of 29 voluntarily submitted phones fits ordinary commercial malware or poor device security, and the committee itself said it could not attribute the malware to Pegasus. The Union's non-cooperation fits the national-security stance it had already taken before the Court. That is not proof that it procured or used the spyware. The claim, read as written, does not assert either point, so this reading does not contradict it.
verdicts.reason: The substance holds. The Wire (2022-08-25) says: "had found 'malware' in five out of the 29 devices submitted to it. The bench also noted that the Union government 'did not cooperate' with the expert committee... the committee found no conclusive proof of whether Pegasus was the malware used". It contains nothing about 29 devices, malware on 5, inconclusive findings or non-cooperation, so it cannot support the claim. The other source is a tertiary Wikipedia page. The claim survives on retrieved press reporting, not on the sources the record actually cites. Two independent outlets (The Wire and Scroll, both also cited by Indian Express) would meet the contract's bar for "documented". Only upgrade once those outlets are attached. With the record's current sources, "reported" is the ceiling.

verdicts.baseRate: This does not discriminate as evidence of anything unusual. Large Indian corruption cases involving politicians very commonly run more than a decade with no trial verdict (2G, Bofors, CWG). Courts quashing prosecution sanction, and governors refusing or granting it, is routine litigation. The claim implies no wrongdoing beyond what the commission found, and it is a factual chronology rather than an inference, so this is acceptable.

verdicts.innocentReading: Quashing the sanction was a procedural ruling: a second sanction needs fresh material, so the ruling is not a finding of innocence. The SC order keeps the status quo while the appeal is pending and is not a judgment on the merits. "No verdict" reflects the pace of the courts, and the case is still pending, not dropped. On symmetry: a UPA-era governor refused sanction (2013), an NDA-era governor granted it (2016), the HC quashed it (2017), and Chavan joined the BJP in Feb 2024. Reading the same facts under both governments gives the same result: an unresolved prosecution under both. Any framing should note the 2024 party switch so the record does not read as targeting one party.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as written: CAG reported in Report No. 4 of 2007 that 60% of cases ended with a single vendor qualified because of how QRs were drafted. The report was tabled in May 2007. Ajai Shukla's contemporaneous Business Standard piece (19 May 2007, on ajaishukla.com) says it was "tabled in Parliament on Monday" and that "The contracts were all signed between January 2003 and March 2006, and relate to equipment only for the army." So the conduct described falls between Jan 2003 and Mar 2006, under both NDA (to May 2004) and UPA-I. Using `from: "2007"` as the event date conflates the report date with the conduct window. No anachronism: ORF (2021-02-04) cites a report that existed by then.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the right one. ORF footnote [9] reads: "'Union Government (Defence Services): Army and Ordnance Factories', Report No. 4 of 2007, Comptroller and Auditor General of India, pp. 10-11", which matches the report number in the claim. The universe is wrong, though. ORF says "QRs prepared by the Indian Army for many of its procurements", and Shukla says the audit "closely scrutinised 37 purchases of equipment from foreign vendors, worth Rs 3,201 crores ... equipment only for the army." The claim says "60% of defence acquisition cases", which implies all defence, or all MoD, acquisition. The finding covers a 37-contract sample of Army foreign purchases (60% is about 22 cases if the base is all 37, but that base is not confirmed). The target `min:ministry-of-defence` is acceptable, since MoD runs Army capital acquisition, but the label needs to name the Army sample.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a single audit sample with no peer comparison in hand. Single-vendor outcomes from over-specified QRs come up again and again in CAG defence audits. ORF itself notes that the 2019 IAF report (No. 3 of 2019) found QRs "vendor-driven" (660 parameters for MMRCA). So the finding describes the whole system and does not single out any one government. The period it covers (2003-06) spans the NDA and UPA-I governments. On the UPA-II vs NDA control, the 2007 (Army 2003-06) and 2019 (IAF) CAG findings read the same way, so the lens is symmetric. No vendor, person or party is named as a beneficiary.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. The MoD's replies are printed inside the CAG report, which could not be reached (cag.gov.in reset the connection on every try, including the thematic-history mirror). Shukla records an MoD reply only on the IOCMH case ("the equipment was urgently required"), not on the 60% figure.
verdicts.innocentReading: Few foreign suppliers make niche Army equipment at all. QRs written for operating conditions found nowhere else (Siachen, high altitude) and a lack of testing facilities can, without any steering, leave one vendor compliant. The CAG framed the problem as an institutional failure: no specialised acquisition organisation, as the Group of Ministers had recommended. It did not say any vendor was favoured.
verdicts.reason: The cited ORF source confirms the figure, word for word: the CAG noted that Army QRs "caused poor competition with 60 percent of cases having a single vendor qualified. [9]", with footnote [9] giving CAG Report No. 4 of 2007, pp. 10-11. That is one credible outlet citing a named primary document, so `reported` is the right tier. Shukla's 2007 piece independently confirms the report and its scope, but not the 60% figure, so the claim cannot be upgraded. The flaw is in scope, not substance. The claim generalises from a 37-contract sample of Army foreign purchases signed 2003-06 to "defence acquisition cases" generally. I'd fix it rather than kill it. The primary report was not read.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Label and text: replace "60% of defence acquisition cases" with "60% of cases in CAG's sample of 37 Army equipment contracts with foreign vendors (Rs 3,201 cr, signed Jan 2003 to Mar 2006) ended with a single vendor qualified; ORF cites pp. 10-11." 2) `from`/`to`: set the conduct window to 2003-01 to 2006-03 and add `reportDate: 2007-05`, or say in `d` that 2007 is the tabling date. 3) Add a second source, Ajai Shukla, Business Standard, 19 May 2007, "CAG criticises army's purchase procedures" (https://www.ajaishukla.com/2007/05/cag-criticises-armys-purchase.html), for scope and sample only, not for the 60% figure. 4) Add `innocentReading` (a niche supplier base and unique operating QRs) and `symmetryCheck`: the window spans NDA and UPA-I, and the 2019 IAF CAG report found the same QR pathology. 5) Keep tier `reported`. Change `upgradeIf` to say the paragraph on pp. 10-11 must be confirmed, including the denominator of the 60%. 6) Note in `d` that the base of "60 percent of cases" (all 37 or a subset) is not confirmed. 7) `pred` 'enforce' is loose for an audit observation; consider an audit/oversight predicate if the contract defines one.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as a sentence: "ORF authors Behera and Kaushal (Issue Brief 567, Aug 2023) estimated that the Agnipath scheme (Cabinet-approved June 2022) saves salary from the first intake, with pension savings coming only after 2044." verdicts.identityTest: Subject force:agnipath is correct. The target min:ministry-of-defence and the phrase "its proponents' own arithmetic" are a problem. The arithmetic belongs to independent ORF analysts arguing for the scheme, not to MoD. DPG says "The government and the military are silent on the issue of manpower savings". The Department of Military Affairs (Lt Gen Anil Puri) has said pension savings were not a consideration. As written, a reader could take the figures to be the ministry's own, and they are not.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not a discrimination claim, so no base rate applies. Symmetry: run the same lens on the 2004 civil-service move to NPS (started under NDA-I, continued under UPA). It gives the same reading: a prospective change that saves little now and defers savings by decades. The lens is party-neutral.
verdicts.denialFound: Partial counter-statement. Lt Gen Anil Puri (DMA) told NDTV that saving on pensions was not a consideration and that his Agniveer analysis had "no financial chapter". This is reported in The Wire, "Why Is the Military Disowning Agnipath's Pension Saving Element?" (https://thewire.in/security/agnipath-scheme-pension-savings-military-denial). It does not dispute the ORF figures; it disputes the motive. No MoD actuarial rebuttal was found. MoD was not asked by this platform.
verdicts.innocentReading: The figures are one think tank's illustrative model, not a government projection. The scheme's stated aim is a younger force, as PRS notes: "While the stated aim of the policy is to enhance the youthful profile of the armed forces, it may also help in reducing pension expenditure in the long term." Changing future contract terms prospectively is lawful, and deferred savings are built into any pension reform.
verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the figures; every one is in the ORF brief verbatim:
- "The monthly average salary of an Agniveer (including the 30-percent contribution ... seva nidhi package) will be INR 45,338"
- "average monthly pay of INR 59,976 of a current OR"
- "INR 175,656 less ... every year"
- "Assuming 60,000 Agniveers are inducted in the first year, the total saving on salaries would amount to INR 1,054 crore"
- "It is only after 2044 that the number of pensioners ... will start declining"
- "only 454,688 (34 percent) of 1.33 million ORs will be entitled to pension"
- "On pensions, however, there will be no savings in the near to medium term."

DPG and PRS back the direction of the claim (DPG: "steady reduction in the salary and pension budget"; PRS: may reduce pension "in the long term"). Neither carries the numbers. Analytic is the right tier for a modelled projection that implies no wrongdoing. The claim survives, but with framing fixes: whose arithmetic it is, the fact that 60,000 is an assumption, the DPG chronology, and the DMA counter-statement.

The 2022-23 Revised Estimate (RE) was ₹1,53,414 cr, about 28% higher, because ₹28,137 cr of OROP arrears were paid that year (PRS DFG 2023-24 analysis, https://prsindia.org/budgets/parliament/demand-for-grants-2023-24-analysis-defence). The source was published in Aug 2023, before 2022-23 actuals existed, so the brief is consistent with what was available to it. Using the RE, the 2013-14 to 2022-23 rise is about 237%, not 163%. The claim as reported actually understates the growth.

Defence pension also roughly doubled under UPA-II: about ₹22k cr (FY2009-10) to about ₹45.5k cr (FY2013-14), after the 6th CPC and its arrears. So fast pension growth does not single out NDA. Symmetry control (UPA-II beside NDA): the same lens shows steep pension growth in both periods, each tied to a pay commission or OROP step. The claim does not assign blame, so it creates no symmetry problem, but the record should not imply that the growth is specific to one regime.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is a descriptive fiscal figure, not an accusation, so there is no party to deny it. MoD's own Demands for Grants and PRS analysis report the same BE figure. No contrary reporting on the 2013-14 figure was found.
verdicts.innocentReading: The step changes follow the 7th CPC (2016) and OROP (2015, revised in 2022 effective 2019), with arrears. These were deliberate policy commitments to retired personnel, and the number of pensioners grew (26.8 lakh in 2021). The record's own innocentReading field fits this.
verdicts.reason: I opened the source and its wording matches the claim: "In the last 10 years (2013-14 to 2022-23), pension expenditure has increased by 163 percent from INR 45,500 crore to INR 119,696 crore ... the MoD's overall expenditure has risen by a far lower 107 percent." Without that note, readers could take ₹1,19,696 cr as the 2022-23 outturn.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as a sentence: India (the importing state; the edge subject is min:ministry-of-defence) was the second-largest arms importer, with an 8.3% share, in 2020–24. Its imports fell 9.3% from 2015–19 to 2020–24, and Russia's share fell from 72% (2010–14) to 36% (2020–24). The record's from/to is 2020–2024, which matches the import rank, the share and the −9.3% change. The "72% → 36%" leg, though, compares 2010–14 with 2020–24 and skips the 2015–19 figure of 55%. Read beside "−9.3% (2015–19 to 2020–24)", it implies Russia's share halved within one window. It actually halved over two windows: 72 to 55 to 36. The window is compressed, but no date is wrong.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity matches. SIPRI names "India" as the recipient state. Table 2, row 2, reads: "India 8.3 9.1 –9.3 Russia 36 France 33 Israel 13". Using min:ministry-of-defence as the subject node is a reasonable stand-in for the procuring state. No person is named.
verdicts.baseRate: The −9.3% fall does not single India out. Over the same period China's imports fell 64%. East Asia fell 22% and South East Asia 45%. Five of the top 10 importers in table 2 show falls between 2015–19 and 2020–24. Being a top-5 importer mostly reflects country size and threat environment. Pakistan, the regional control, rose 61% and has 81% from China, so the same lens gives the opposite reading there, which points to the data rather than the lens. India's Russian share falling while France (33%) and Israel (13%) rise is specific to India. SIPRI itself treats it as a trend.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is a descriptive statistic and accuses no one. I did not ask MoD for a response. SIPRI's own reading partly matches the record's innocentReading: "The drop was at least partly the result of India's increasing ability to design and produce its own weapons, making it less reliant on imports." I found no contrary reporting on these figures.
verdicts.innocentReading: SIPRI's trend-indicator values (TIV) measure delivered volume, not money spent, and five-year windows swing with lumpy deliveries. The 2020–22 Rafale deliveries, for example, raised France's share. A modest fall plus a diversifying supplier base fits indigenisation, the post-2022 cut in Russian export capacity (SIPRI notes Russia prioritised its own forces) and timing of individual deliveries. A high rank follows from India's size and the two-front threat.
verdicts.reason: I opened the SIPRI fact sheet (fs_2503_at_2024.pdf, "India and Pakistan" section and table 2), and it states every figure in the claim. Quote: "India was the world's second largest arms importer in 2020–24 with an 8.3 per cent share of global imports. Indian arms imports decreased by 9.3 per cent between 2015–19 and 2020–24... The largest share of India's imports came from Russia (36 per cent); however, this was a significantly smaller share than in 2015–19 (55 per cent) and 2010–14 (72 per cent)." The France 33% and Israel 13% figures in the record's d field are confirmed by table 2. Nothing is invented, and the claim does not combine separate facts to imply wrongdoing. The only defect is that the "72% → 36%" label leaves out the time windows. The "analytic" tier is right for putting the import rank beside the falling trend, and the claim carries an innocentReading. If the claim were cut down to the bare figures, it could be raised to documented.
verdicts.corrections: 1. text/lab: replace "Russia's share 72% → 36%" with "Russia's share 72% (2010–14) → 55% (2015–19) → 36% (2020–24)". The windows need to be explicit so the halving is not read as falling inside the −9.3% window. 2. d: add that SIPRI measures volume in trend-indicator values (TIV), not spending, and that the figures are 5-year aggregates sensitive to delivery timing. 3. Optionally set from to "2010" for the Russian-share leg, or keep 2020–2024 and rely on the explicit windows in the text. 4. innocentReading: add SIPRI's other explanation, Russia putting its own forces first after 2022, alongside indigenisation. 5. The killIf condition "imports rising again" should say which measure it means: TIV share or rank for 2021–25.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is "BPR&D (via PRS) records 155 actual police per lakh on 2023-01-01, which is 70% of 222 and 86% of the sanctioned ratio of 181 from January 2016". The numerator date is confirmed by PRS DFG 2025-26 Home Affairs (p.12): "As of January 2023, India has 155 police personnel for every one lakh people", and Table 15 (as on January 1, 2023): "India 155", sourced to BPR&D DoPO, March 2024. The denominator date is confirmed by PRS 2017: "while the sanctioned police strength was 181 police per lakh persons in 2016, the actual strength was 137 police." The arithmetic holds: 155/222 = 0.698 and 155/181 = 0.856. The problem is that the two figures come from different years. The claim divides a 2023 actual by a 2016 sanctioned ratio, and that sanction has since been raised. MoS Home Nityanand Rai said in a Lok Sabha written reply on 28 March 2023 (reported by The Federal) that "the ratio for the whole country as on January 1, 2022 ... is 196.23 as per sanctioned strength and 152.80 as per actual strength." A Business Standard post of March 2025 gives 154.84 actual against 196.88 sanctioned for 2023. That post returned 402 and was not opened. Against the sanction in force at the time, 2023 actual strength is about 79% (155/196.9), not 86%. The claim does label the denominator "2016", so it is not false. But read as "the shortfall against India's own sanction", it understates the gap: about 21%, not 14%.
verdicts.identityTest: The figures are the right ones: all-India police per lakh from BPR&D Data on Police Organisations, total state and UT police (civil, armed, DAR, IRB), the same series in 2016 and 2023. The edge source node is min:ministry-of-home-affairs. That is acceptable, since BPR&D sits under MHA and PRS is analysing the MHA demand, but most of the 155 are state police, which is a state subject. The ratio describes the states' forces, not MHA's own. The target node force:lit-un-222-benchmark correctly carries "unverified".
verdicts.baseRate: This is a single national ratio, not a property shared across a set of entities, so the 80% test does not apply in the usual way. From PRS Table 15, roughly half of states and UTs (mostly small, NE and border units: Nagaland 1,136, A&N 1,050, Manipur 942) are at or above 222. The large states are below it: Bihar 81, WB 101, MP 121, Odisha 121, Rajasthan 118, Gujarat 124, UP 135, Maharashtra 137. Falling short of 222 does not separate BJP-run states from opposition-run ones; both groups are on both sides. The 222 figure itself has no UN instrument behind it. PRS 2017 cites it without a source, and Africa Check's fact-check page (403, not opened; search snippet only) calls a UN police ratio a myth.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and nobody was asked. MHA's own Lok Sabha reply (28 Mar 2023) gives sanctioned 196.23 and actual 152.80 for 2022-01-01 and does not cite a UN norm. No government statement disputes 155, and none claims a UN source for 222.
verdicts.innocentReading: Police need depends on crime, terrain, urbanisation and insurgency, so a national ratio is a rule of thumb. 222 is a figure that circulates without a UN source. The states' own sanctioned strength (about 196 per lakh by 2022–23) is their declared need. Actual strength has risen from 137 (2016) to 155 (2023) while sanctions rose from 181 to about 196, so the vacancy rate has stayed around 20–24%. That points to slow state recruitment, not a cut.
verdicts.reason: Both sources, opened directly, say exactly what the claim uses (155 as on 2023-01-01; 181 sanctioned and 137 actual in 2016; 222 "UN recommended"), and the arithmetic is right. The claim also flags 222 as unverified, so it is an honest analytic comparison and survives. Its weak point is the second ratio. Dividing a 2023 actual by a 2016 sanction is a mixed-vintage comparison and overstates sanctioned-post fill. MHA's own Parliament answer gives a sanctioned 196.23 for 2022 (about 196.9 for 2023, reported but not opened), which puts the contemporaneous ratio at about 79%. This needs correcting, but it does not refute the claim, because the label says "2016".
verdicts.corrections: 1. lab/text: change "86% of the 2016 sanctioned ratio (181)" to "about 79% of the sanctioned ratio in force (196.23 on 2022-01-01 per MHA Lok Sabha reply of 2023-03-28; about 196.9 on 2023-01-01 reported), and 86% of the 2016 sanction (181)". Or drop the 2016 comparison. 2. srcs: add the 28 Mar 2023 Lok Sabha written reply (MoS Nityanand Rai), via https://thefederal.com/news/bihar-west-bengal-have-lowest-police-public-ratio-govt or the sansad.in answer, for the contemporaneous sanctioned ratio. 3. d: add that the 2016 sanction has been superseded, so the vacancy-adjusted shortfall is about 21%, not 14%. The baseRates row with denominator 181 should either pair 137/181 (same year, as now) or add 152.80/196.23 (2022). SPIR 2019 was published in 2019, but its state figure uses BPR&D data from 2016: Table 1.2 gives "All-India 77.4" (overall actual as % of sanctioned, as of 2016), and Table 1.1 gives a 2012-16 average of 75.2. The CAPF figure is from 2024-07-01 (PRS Table 4, from LS Unstarred Q 2426, 6 Aug 2024). That is an 8-year gap, and the record's from/to of 2016-2024 hides it. The record's own killIf asks for BPR&D 2023/2024 data, which exists. The India Justice Report 2025 (from BPR&D DoPO 1.1.2023) puts state vacancies at about 21-22%, so the gap still holds roughly and the killIf is not triggered. Still, a same-year comparison is available and should be used.
verdicts.identityTest: Actor: MHA (Union). Thing: filling of CAPF sanctioned posts. Compared against: all state and UT police, as aggregated by BPR&D. The CAPF figure of 90.5% is not printed in PRS. It is derived from five forces (CISF, CRPF, ITBP, SSB, BSF): 9,80,215 sanctioned and 8,87,543 actual, which gives 0.9055. PRS's own row covers all CAPFs including Assam Rifles: "Total 10,45,751 9,50,118 9%" (90.9% filled). PRS's text says "As of July 1, 2024, 9% of posts across all CAPFs are vacant." The arithmetic checks, but the claim should say "five CAPFs excluding AR" or use PRS's 9%. The state side is also not purely "the states". The BPR&D all-India total includes Delhi Police, which is under MHA control and 98.3% filled, plus other UT police. So part of the "state" figure is actually the Union's own force.
verdicts.baseRate: State fill rates in 2016 (SPIR Table 1.2) ranged from 48.1% (UP) to 107.2% (Nagaland). Eight states were above 90% (Nagaland, Delhi, Kerala, HP, Uttarakhand, TN, Maharashtra, Punjab), which is at or above the CAPF figure. So "states fill less" is an average that hides wide variation, and it is driven heavily by UP (48%), Bihar, Jharkhand, Gujarat, WB and Haryana. Symmetry: the low and high groups both mix BJP-run and opposition-run states. In 2016, UP (SP) and Gujarat (BJP) were low; Kerala (LDF) and Maharashtra (BJP) were high. So the comparison has no partisan slant. The Union is not uniformly better either. The same PRS document says NDRF (Union) had 18,557 sanctioned and 14,197 actual, "amounting to a 23% vacancy rate" (Jan 2023). That equals the state police rate. CISF is at 19%, close to the state average.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; nobody was asked. This is an analytic comparison with no wrongdoing alleged, so no denial is needed. MHA's stated position in Parliament (LS UQ 2426, 2024) is that vacancies are being filled, including the 10% reservation for ex-Agniveers (PRS: "In order to address vacancies, 10% of constable/rifleman positions in the CAPFs and AR have been reserved for ex-Agniveers").
verdicts.innocentReading: Several things fit the gap without implying better management at the Union level. CAPFs recruit centrally through SSC with one paymaster, while state recruitment is scattered and often held up in court (SPIR itself cites UP's 41,610-constable drive of 2013). State sanctioned strengths are paper numbers that are often raised without funding. The years compared are different (2016 vs 2024). And the large states (UP, Bihar) dominate the all-India denominator.
verdicts.reason: The headline inference is arithmetically false. 90.5% filled against 77% filled means the Union fills its forces about 1.18 times as fully, not "about twice as fully." What is roughly 2.4x is the vacancy rate (23% vs 9.5%). The text and the "d" field ("The Union fills its own forces about twice as fully as the states fill theirs") turn a vacancy ratio into a fill ratio and overstate the gap by about a factor of 6 in relative terms. The source numbers themselves hold: SPIR says "The police in India works at 77 percent of its sanctioned strength", and the PRS Table 4 figures sum to the five-CAPF totals. But they come from years 8 apart, the CAPF figure is derived rather than printed, and the state side includes the Union-run Delhi Police. Once corrected, the comparison survives as analytic. As written, it is refuted.
verdicts.corrections: text/d: replace "the Union fills its forces about twice as fully as the states" with "state police vacancy (23%, 2016 data) is about 2.4 times the CAPF vacancy (9.5%, 2024); fill rates are 77% vs 90.5%." Label the state figure "SPIR 2019, BPR&D data as of 2016 (77.4%; 2012-16 average 75.2%)". Label the CAPF figure "five CAPFs excl. Assam Rifles, derived from PRS Table 4 (all CAPFs incl. AR: 9% vacant, 90.9% filled)". Add to innocentReading: the all-India state figure includes the MHA-controlled Delhi Police (98.3%); 8 of 23 states were above 90% in 2016; Union-run NDRF had 23% vacancy (Jan 2023) and CISF 19%. Replace the state figure with BPR&D DoPO 1.1.2023 or 2024 (about 21-22% vacancy per India Justice Report 2025) for a closer-in-time comparison. The from/to should note that the two endpoints are 2016 and 2024-07-01, not a continuous period. Keep the tier as analytic.

verdicts.reason: The PRS PDF states every figure in the claim, quoted verbatim, with Table 8 as on Jan 1, 2023, sourced to BPR&D DoPO. No inference, conjunction or wrongdoing is implied. The subject node "wel:lokniti-csds" covers only one of the two co-publishers. The SPEC's UPA-II vs NDA control cannot be run either, because the instrument has no pre-2018 baseline. The record's innocentReading already says this. The claim does not single out any state or party, so the symmetry test does not arise. One caution: SPIR 2025 has state-level breakdowns (for example Tamil Nadu 45%, Odisha). verdicts.denialFound: No institutional denial from the MHA or any state police was found, and none was sought by this record. At the launch, former DGP Prakash Singh disputed the definition of torture ("What is torture? In India there is no definition of torture. Does a slap constitute torture? I don't think so") and stressed that most respondents back legal procedure and human-rights training (https://www.livelaw.in/articles/launch-status-policing-report-india-report-2025-police-torture-288708). LeDroit India published a critique of bias and flaws in the method (https://ledroitindia.in/status-of-policing-in-india-report-2025-bias-flaws/). The report itself flags social-desirability bias (SPIR 2025, p.24, fn 1).
verdicts.innocentReading: These are self-reported attitudes collected in face-to-face interviews. They may overstate or understate real behaviour, and none of them measures how often torture happens. Prakash Singh's objection also fits: questions that group "slapping" with torture inflate how much support for torture appears. The SPIR 2018 question ("There is nothing wrong in the police being violent towards criminals") does not mention custody in its wording. Only the figure title adds "in police custody".
verdicts.reason: Two of the figures in the claim do not match the source as written. (1) "~1 in 10 justify third degree" picks the lowest number and drops its qualifier. SPIR 2025 Fig. 5.7 is about witnesses: "nearly one in every ten police personnel (9%) justify the use of third-degree methods against an 'uncooperative' witness". The other 9% is for petty offences. The report's headline figure is Table 5.3: "Thirty percent police personnel said that 'third-degree methods' are justified towards the accused in serious criminal cases". Fig. 5.9 adds "Nearly two-thirds ... justified to deal with an uncooperative accused in case of kidnapping". Unqualified, the claim understates the source's main finding by a factor of three. (2) The "11% justify hitting an absconder's family" figure is the "absolutely justified" share only. The source says "two in five of the police personnel justify 'hitting or slapping' the family members of absconding suspects ... of which 11 percent said that it is absolutely justified and another 30 percent said that it is sometimes justified." These figures are confirmed verbatim: 30% on lawyers ("30 percent of the police personnel believe that lawyers should never be present during interrogation"), 70% on confessions (Table 4.9), and SPIR 2018 "Half the respondents condone the use of violence on criminals in police custody" (Fig. 5.7, p.99; fully agree plus somewhat agree = 50%). The "attitudes, not incidence" framing is correct. Once the figures are corrected, the claim holds at the "reported" tier: a credible think-tank and academic report with a published method appendix.

Replace "11% justify hitting an absconder's family" with "11% call hitting an absconder's family 'absolutely justified', 41% justified at least sometimes".

Add the sample: "8,276 police personnel, 82 locations, 16 states + NCT Delhi". Add a contra/denial field: Prakash Singh's definitional objection (LiveLaw URL above), plus "MHA/state police not asked; no institutional response found".
pred "analytic" alongside tier "reported" is acceptable, provided the edge is described as source-reported survey rates rather than our own inference.
killIf: keep. upgradeIf: keep.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as: Chalfin & McCrary (authors) estimated a police elasticity of cost-weighted crime of about -0.5 (thing) for medium and large US cities, 1960-2010, in NBER WP 18815, February 2013 (when). The claim's "from: 2013" matches the paper date. The sample window (1960-2010) is stated correctly. Because there is no actor tenure, the overlap test does not apply. The paper was later published as "Are U.S. Cities Underpoliced?" (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2018), and the field could record that as the durable citation. This does not invalidate the 2013 date.
verdicts.identityTest: The paper's identity is right: NBER w18815, authors Aaron Chalfin and Justin McCrary, title "The Effect of Police on Crime: New Evidence from U.S. Cities, 1960-2010". The target "min:ministry-of-home-affairs" only places the benchmark in the domain. The paper says nothing about the MHA, and the claim's own d-text and innocentReading say the estimate does not transfer to India. Nobody below public rank is named, and the claim contains no budget or operational detail.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable as a discrimination test. This is a scoping claim about one benchmark and says nothing about the property of any Indian entity. Most US quasi-experimental studies (Levitt, Evans & Owens, Di Tella & Schargrodsky, Draca et al.) find negative police-crime elasticities. So the claim that more police reduce crime is the consensus, not a finding that singles anyone out, and the record says no more than that.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim accuses no party. No response was sought or needed.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record already carries it: carrying a US elasticity over to Indian states is unwarranted, Indian strength data are state-level, and vacancies rather than head counts drive variation. Read plainly, the claim only says what one US paper finds and that the sweep opened no Indian estimate (the Mathen 2025 paper returned a 403). It implies no wrongdoing and does not endorse any particular ratio, such as 222 per lakh.
verdicts.reason: I opened https://www.nber.org/papers/w18815. The abstract finds that "police reduce violent crime more so than property crime" and that measurement-error-corrected estimates give a police elasticity of about -0.5 for the cost-weighted sum of crimes in medium-to-large US cities, 1960-2010. The amount, sign, unit (cost-weighted crime), place and period all match the claim. The second half of the claim ("no Indian estimate opened") is a statement about the sweep, not a claim that no Indian estimate exists, and the record documents it (Wiley 403 on DOI 10.1002/pa.70043). The claim does not combine true facts into an implied accusation. In fact it explicitly blocks the inference from the US figure to India. Tier analytic is correct for a scoping inference, and the required innocentReading is present. No refusal in CONTRACT-force is triggered, and the SPEC controls (UPA/NDA, BJP vs opposition states, vendor vs DPSU) do not apply to a literature benchmark.
verdicts.corrections: These are optional. (1) In the short text, change "no Indian estimate opened" to "no Indian estimate opened in this sweep (Mathen 2025, DOI 10.1002/pa.70043, Wiley 403)" so it cannot be read as "none exists". (2) Add the published version as a second source: Chalfin & McCrary, "Are U.S. Cities Underpoliced? Theory and Evidence", Review of Economics and Statistics 100(1), 2018. (3) Write "cost-weighted crime" in the short text to match the paper's unit. Plain "crime" overstates it, because the paper's violent and property elasticities differ. (4) Add a symmetryCheck note saying the party and state controls do not apply to a literature benchmark. Keep the tier at analytic.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: Behera (MP-IDSA) reported, in an Issue Brief of 4 Feb 2020, the gap between MoD's resource projection and its allocation for FY2013-14 through FY2019-20. The figures come before the publication date, and the brief is the author's own (it carries his byline). The 2019-20 figure must be the BE or RE allocation, since the year had not closed. The period covers UPA-II (2013-14) and NDA (2014-15 onward). The source assigns no actor tenure and claims no causal link, so there is no overlap problem to test.
verdicts.identityTest: The source is the MP-IDSA Issue Brief "India's Defence Budget 2020-21" by Laxman Kumar Behera, dated 4 Feb 2020. The URL resolves to that document. The subject is MoD, specifically "Figure 1: MoD's Resource Projection and Allocation under Defence Services Estimates". Calling it the "services'" gap is acceptable because the DSE is the services' budget. But the source's own words are "MoD's gap between resource requirement and allocation".
verdicts.baseRate: Every year in the series shows a gap, ranging from 14% to 30%. Projections exceed allocations under every government, so the existence of a gap tells you nothing on its own. Only the changes over time carry information. The series is symmetric across governments: the UPA-II year (2013-14, 27%) is roughly as high as the NDA years 2018-19 (30%) and 2019-20 (25%), and the lowest point (2015-16, 14%) also falls under NDA. Applying the same lens to UPA-II produces the same reading.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was sought. The claim accuses no one of wrongdoing; it states a measured budget shortfall. MoD's usual position in Standing Committee replies is that it will seek additional funds at the RE stage, but I did not find a reply addressed to this brief.
verdicts.innocentReading: The services' projections are what they ask for, not an independent measure of need, and they routinely exceed what the fiscal space allows under any government. A gap is the normal state of defence budgeting and does not by itself show neglect. Behera himself puts it down to a fiscal squeeze: GDP growth at an eight-year low and lower tax revenue.
verdicts.reason: The source says exactly what the claim says. The quoted passage is: "In the past seven years, MoD's gap between resource requirement and allocation, which briefly narrowed from a high of 27 per cent in 2013-14 to 14 per cent in 2015-16, has increased to 30 per cent in 2018-19 and 25 per cent in 2019-20 (see Figure 1)." I recomputed the gaps from what I read as the projection and allocation figures in Figure 1 of the PDF text. They match: 280341/203672 gives 27.3%, 287386/246727 gives 14.1%, 401044/282733 gives 29.5%, and 405785/305296 gives 24.8%. The underlying data is MoD/DSE figures as Standing Committee reports usually present them, but the claim rests on one named-author think-tank analysis. That fits "reported", not "documented", until the committee tables themselves are opened. No person, operational detail or unpublished budget is named, so there is no reason to kill it.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Change the wording from "Services' projection-vs-allocation gap" to "MoD's resource projection vs allocation gap under Defence Services Estimates", which is the source's own phrasing in Figure 1. 2. State that the four years are the author's selected points and that Figure 1 also plots 2014-15, 2016-17 and 2017-18. My reading of the figure is about 26% for 2014-15 and values in the 15–20% range for 2016-17 and 2017-18. The text extraction was too scrambled to tell which of those two years is which, so check the figure before recording them. 3. Add that the 2019-20 allocation is a budget-stage (BE) figure. 4. In the entity record, change the tier on the gap-series statement in the "Establishes" line from [documented] to [reported], to match the edge tier, because the only source is the IDSA brief. 5. The PRS 2025-26 source on the edge does support the ₹9.01 lakh crore capital-outlay statement in "d" (PRS: "the Ministry estimated to receive Rs 9.01 lakh crore for capital outlay against the defence plan projection"). It does not support the 2013-20 gap series, so do not cite it for the claim text. 6. Keep upgradeIf as it is: Standing Committee on Defence report tables on sansad.in.

verdicts.dateTest: Partly passes. Bofors: Swedish Radio story on 16 Apr 1987, confirmed by the Wikipedia page. Delhi HC judgment by J.D. Kapoor J. dated 4 Feb 2004, confirmed on Indian Kanoon doc 561739. Rafale: SC judgment of 14 Dec 2018, confirmed on Indian Kanoon doc 95183857. French judge appointed in June 2021, confirmed by Wikipedia: "In June 2021, a French judge was appointed to lead a judicial investigation into alleged corruption and favoritism in the deal." Two dates are not supported by any cited source. (1) The MoD note of 24 Nov 2015 (the S.K. Sharma note on the PMO's parallel negotiations) does not appear on the Rafale Wikipedia page, and none of the four srcs carries it. It needs The Hindu (N. Ram, 8 Feb 2019) as a source. (2) "The Hindu 1987" for Bofors is loose. Swedish Radio broke the story in April 1987, and The Hindu's document series (Chitra Subramaniam / N. Ram) ran from 1987 to 1989. The Bofors milestone that best matches "court declining to find wrongdoing" is actually 31 May 2005 (R.S. Sodhi J., charges against the Hindujas and Bofors quashed), not 4 Feb 2004.
verdicts.identityTest: Fails for the Bofors court field. The 2004 Delhi HC judgment (Kartongen Kemi Och Forvaltning AB v State through CBI, 2004(72)DRJ693) was a petition by AB Bofors and the Hinduja brothers. It did not decline to find wrongdoing. It quashed the PC Act conspiracy and abetment charges but directed that charges "need to be framed against the petitioners P.P. Hinduja, G.P. Hinduja and S.P. Hinduja for the offences punishable under Sections 120B / 420 IPC". It also stated that the CBI "succeeded in tracing the Swiss accounts of 'Commission Agents' employed by M/s A.B. Bofors wherein illegal payments received by them from Bofors as commission were deposited." The "no evidence ... received pay-offs" line is the Special Judge's observation about public servants, which the HC quotes; it is not a general finding of no wrongdoing. The two court acts are also different kinds of thing. Bofors was a criminal trial process: FIR 1990, chargesheet 1999, charges framed 14.11.2002. The Rafale ruling was an Article 32 judicial review that declined to order an FIR at all: "we find no reason for any intervention by this Court ... We, thus, dismiss all the writ petitions."
verdicts.baseRate: Not discriminating, and the record itself says so. Of the five fields, "no conviction of an Indian public servant" and "a court declines to intervene or quashes" fit nearly every major Indian defence-procurement controversy (AgustaWestland, Tatra/BEML, HDW submarines, Barak). Most of them also have a foreign probe (Italy for AgustaWestland, Germany for HDW). Those two or three fields are therefore close to universal (80% or more) and carry no information. The fields that could tell the cases apart are where they differ. Bofors has payments shown in the paper trail (Swiss accounts, Swedish National Audit Bureau 1987, Bofors's own admission of "winding-up" payments to agents) and an Indian prosecution. Rafale has a process anomaly (the MoD note on PMO parallel talks, removal of anti-corruption clauses), no Indian FIR, and a 2019 CAG report (Report No. 3 of 2019) that found the price 2.86% lower than the 2007 offer.
verdicts.denialFound: The responses are on record but none was pulled into this record. Rafale: Defence Minister Sitharaman denied procedural wrongdoing and said CCS approval preceded the IGA (cited on the Rafale Wikipedia page). Dassault and the GoI rejected the Mediapart and PNF allegations. Bofors: Rajiv Gandhi denied in Parliament in 1987 that he or his family received money, and the Hindujas denied throughout. The claim should cite at least one response per side. None was asked by this platform.
verdicts.innocentReading: Big-ticket foreign arms purchases in India regularly draw allegations, leaked files, PILs and foreign investigations. Indian courts rarely convict because of evidence held abroad, the deaths of accused, delay, and deference to the executive on defence. That a scandal and a non-scandal "end the same way" is a finding about Indian criminal process, not proof that the two cases are equally strong. Bofors had documented illegal commissions. Rafale, as of the record, has no documented payment to an Indian official.
verdicts.reason: The decisive problem is that the claim's own Bofors court source contradicts the "court declining to find wrongdoing" field. The 4 Feb 2004 Delhi HC judgment records "illegal payments" of commission into Swiss accounts and sends 120B/420 charges against the Hindujas to trial. The fields are also asymmetric in substance: Bofors had documented payments and an Indian prosecution, while Rafale has a process anomaly and a refused FIR. Calling this the "same record shape" flattens a difference in evidentiary weight. The pairing is still a valid symmetry control under SPEC ("Bofors beside Rafale — identical fields"), so it should stay analytic, but with each field filled in honestly, differences included. As written, it overstates the parallel and leans on an unsourced date.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Court field, Bofors: change "Delhi HC 2004: no evidence of receipt" to "Delhi HC 4 Feb 2004 (Kapoor J.): no evidence that public servants received pay-offs, but illegal commission payments to agents traced to Swiss accounts; PC Act charges quashed, 120B/420 charges against the Hindujas sustained; all charges against the Hindujas and Bofors quashed 31 May 2005 (Sodhi J.)". Add a source for 2005 and for the SC's 2018 dismissal of the CBI appeal over delay. 2. Process-anomaly field, Bofors: "agent payments in Swiss accounts" is a documented payment, not a process anomaly. Relabel it ("documented payments to agents") so the asymmetry with Rafale (process anomaly, no documented payment to an Indian official) is visible. 3. Add a field "Indian criminal case": Bofors yes (FIR 1990, chargesheet 1999); Rafale no (SC declined an FIR on 14 Dec 2018; review dismissed Nov 2019). 4. Add a field "audit": CAG 1989 on Bofors; CAG Report No. 3 of 2019 on Rafale (price 2.86% lower). Fix upgradeIf: "audit finding lands" has already happened in both cases. 5. Add The Hindu, 8 Feb 2019 (N. Ram) as the source for the MoD note of 24 Nov 2015; it is not in the four srcs. 6. Document trail, Bofors: change to "Swedish Radio 16 Apr 1987; The Hindu document series 1987–89". 7. Foreign probe, Bofors: name the Swedish National Audit Bureau (1987) and the Swedish police inquiry; the Swiss documents came through letters rogatory, not a Swiss probe. 8. Change the label from "same record shape" to "parallel record fields with stated asymmetries", and add one denial per side (Sitharaman/MoD; Rajiv Gandhi 1987).

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out: the CBI opened cases in AgustaWestland and in Tatra in 2012–13 while A.K. Antony was Defence Minister (Oct 2006 to May 2014). The dates overlap. AgustaWestland: the contract was signed in Feb 2010, Orsi was arrested on 2013-02-12, Antony ordered a CBI probe on 2013-02-12/13, the CBI preliminary enquiry is dated 2013-02-25 and the FIR 2013-03-13, all from the Wikipedia article. Tatra: the bribe offer is alleged to have been made on 2010-09-22 and became public in March 2012. The CBI case against Lt Gen Tejinder Singh under section 12 of the Prevention of Corruption Act was registered in Oct 2012 (TheNewsMinute). Both exposures and both CBI cases fall inside UPA-II, so "UPA-era CBI cases from 2012–13" holds. One caveat: the Tatra purchases themselves (about 7,000 trucks over more than two decades, through BEML) began in 1986 and ran through NDA-I (1998–2004). "UPA-era" therefore describes the CBI case and when it came to light, not the procurement window. The record should say so, so the pairing is not read as a UPA-only procurement failure.
