What sets AgustaWestland apart from comparable cases is a set of facts most cases lack: the government cancelled the contract for breach of the integrity pact and recovered ₹2,068 crore; the sitting Defence Minister said on record 'Yes, corruption has taken place in the helicopter deal and bribes have been taken'; an Italian appellate conviction was later overturned; a former service chief was arrested and chargesheeted; and a middleman was extradited. Symmetry check: Rafale (NDA) is rated 'unsupported' and AgustaWestland (UPA) 'contested'. The difference follows the evidence: Rafale has no chargesheet, no cancellation and no ministerial admission, while both have Italian or French acquittals or open probes. Tatra, the control case, is a stub, so the pair cannot yet be compared like for like.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, but none is recorded in the narrative row. (1) The UPA government initially 'denied all allegations and claimed it had "nothing to hide" and that "our track record is not cover-up."' (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Indian_helicopter_bribery_scandal). (2) Michel 'denied any wrongdoing by stating that he had never met any "Gandhi" in his life' (same page). (3) In 2019 the Congress, through Randeep Surjewala, called the ED chargesheet page 'a cheap election stunt'. Ahmed Patel denied wrongdoing and was not named in the CBI FIR (https://www.thequint.com/explainers/explainer-vvip-chopper-scam-agustawestland-congress-bjp-indian-air-force-sp-tyagi; https://www.business-standard.com/article/pti-stories/michel-identified-ap-as-ahmed-patel-ed-chargesheet-in-agustawestland-case-119040401499_1.html). (4) Tyagi has repeatedly denied the allegations.
verdicts.innocentReading: Middlemen promise to pay or influence senior figures in order to justify their fees. Michel's note can be read as a sales pitch or a target list, not proof that money arrived; the note itself says these people were to be 'targeted'. Italy's final acquittal (2018, upheld 2019) found insufficient proof of corruption. The service-ceiling change was a joint SPG/NSA/IAF decision with an operational rationale, namely the expansion of the field beyond one vendor. The cancellation was a contract remedy for an integrity-pact breach by the vendor, not a finding that Indian officials took money. Against this, Defence Minister Antony's own statement that 'bribes have been taken' and the encashed guarantees show that some corruption around the deal was accepted by the UPA government itself. The innocent reading covers who received money, not whether any was paid.
verdicts.reason: The 'contested' rating holds up. A narrative row cannot be documented: the underlying assertion that bribes reached UPA leaders and the IAF chief comes from CBI and ED chargesheets, Italian prosecutors and a middleman's note, and it is answered by final Italian acquittals and an Indian trial that has not begun. That makes it an allegation carrying a counter, which is what 'contested' means. Nothing in the source contradicts the rating, and the dates and identities line up. The row cannot pass as written, though. It cites one Wikipedia page, which does not contain the service-ceiling claim; that claim is a CBI chargesheet allegation reported by the Deccan Chronicle. Its counter repeats Wikipedia's error that Busto Arsizio 'acquitted the former IAF chief', when Tyagi was not a defendant in Italy. It says the trial is 'pending' when it has not commenced. It leaves out the strongest fact for the claim, Antony's on-record 'bribes have been taken', and it records no denial, although Congress, Patel, Tyagi and Michel all denied. The status stands, but the fields must be corrected.
verdicts.corrections: strongestCase: (1) Mark 'the altitude requirement was lowered before the tender' as a CBI allegation and cite it: the 2017-09-01 chargesheet says Tyagi conspired to cut the service ceiling from 6,000 m to 4,500 m (Deccan Chronicle, https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/current-affairs/010917/agustawestland-case-cbi-files-chargesheet-against-ex-iaf-chief-sp-tyagi.html). The Wikipedia page does not say it. (2) Add Defence Minister A.K. Antony's statement 'Yes, corruption has taken place in the helicopter deal and bribes have been taken' (on the Wikipedia page). (3) Say that the note lists Manmohan Singh and others as advisors 'to target', and that 'AP' (€3m) was identified as Ahmed Patel by Michel per the ED chargesheet. strongestCounter: (4) Replace 'the Busto Arsizio court acquitted the former IAF chief in 2014' with 'the Busto Arsizio court (Oct 2014) acquitted Orsi and Spagnolini of corruption, convicting only on false invoicing, and found no proof against Tyagi, who was not a defendant in Italy'. (5) Replace 'the Indian trial is pending after twelve years' with 'the Indian trial had not commenced as of the SC's Feb 2025 bail order (FIR 2013-03-13)'. (6) Add 'Haschke finally acquitted, Brescia appeal court, 2025-06-30'. Add a contra or denial field: the UPA government's 'nothing to hide' (2013), Congress's 'cheap election stunt' (2019), Patel's denial and absence from the FIR, Tyagi's denial, and Michel's 'never met any Gandhi'. claim text: change 'the top of the UPA government' to 'senior UPA-era officials and a Congress party office-holder', or keep the current wording only as the narrative's popular phrasing. srcs: add the Deccan Chronicle chargesheet report and the SC bail order (Deccan Herald https://www.deccanherald.com/india/agustawestland-case-supreme-court-grants-bail-to-middleman-christian-michel-james-3410636) so the row does not rest on Wikipedia alone. The same Tyagi-acquittal error appears in node force:case-agustawestland d[0] and edge literature:c013 and should be fixed there too.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated, the claim is: "Commentators and the Standing Committee on Defence (2018) say India under-spends and should spend 3% of GDP. Measured against FY2025-26 BE (PRS, 4 Feb 2025) and calendar 2024 (SIPRI, Apr 2025), the claim is contested." The dates line up. The SC recommendation is 2018. PRS describes the period after it ("over the last decade ... consistently been lower than this recommended level"). The 15th FC memo covers 2021-26. SIPRI covers 2024. One mismatch: PRS's own SIPRI table is for 2023 (India 4th, $84bn, 2.4%), while the record cites the 2024 fact sheet (5th, $86.1bn, 2.3%). Both are correct for their own year. The UPA control is missing. PRS Fig. 2 starts in 2013-14 (UPA's last year), and capital share was 32% in 2013-14 against "less than 30%" in 2014-15 to 2024-25. SIPRI shows India at 2.5% in 2015 against 2.3% in 2024. The gap to 3% therefore predates 2014 and is not a feature of one government. The narrative should say so.
verdicts.identityTest: The actors are institutions, and they are named correctly: Standing Committee on Defence (2018), Ministry of Defence, PRS (Tushar Chakrabarty), SIPRI. One misattribution. The record says "the Ministry reports committed-liability shortfalls", but PRS attributes that to the Standing Committee on Defence (2019): "The Standing Committee on Defence (2019) expressed concern over the shortage in allocation to meet committed liabilities expenditure." What the Ministry itself reported was the capital shortfall in its 15th Finance Commission memo: "the Ministry estimated to receive Rs 9.01 lakh crore for capital outlay against the defence plan projection of Rs 17.46 lakh crore (48% shortfall)". It also said this led to "serious capability gaps". The two percentages are not the same measure. PRS's 1.9% is the MoD budget including pension, and about 1.4% without pension ("decreases by about 0.5 percentage point"). SIPRI's 2.3% includes paramilitary forces (PRS note: "India's military spending includes expenditure on paramilitary forces"). The counter sets SIPRI's 2.3% against a 3% target framed on the MoD budget, which compares unlike things. The real dispute is mostly about what counts as defence spending (the numerator), not only the GDP denominator.
verdicts.baseRate: Among SIPRI's top 15 spenders in 2024, 9 of 15 are below 3%: Japan 1.4, Italy 1.6, China 1.7, Germany 1.9, Australia 1.9, France 2.1, India 2.3, UK 2.3, South Korea 2.6. Six are at or above 3%: US 3.4, Poland 4.2, Russia 7.1, Saudi Arabia 7.3, Israel 8.8, Ukraine 34. Being under 3% is therefore common (60%) but not universal, so it does not single India out. The record's "median of the fifteen largest = 2.3%" is correct: the 8th of 15 sorted values is 2.3. But that is our own computation, not something SIPRI says. "World average 2.5%" is SIPRI's global military burden (world spending divided by world GDP, weighted towards the US). It is not an average across countries. SIPRI's actual per-country averages are 1.9% for countries not in armed conflict and 4.4% for countries in armed conflict, so India's 2.3% sits between the two. Pakistan, the neighbour comparator, is at 2.7%.
verdicts.denialFound: The government's response is already in the cited PRS source, and the record leaves it out. PRS p.2: "According to the Ministry of Defence, spending 3% of India's GDP on the defence sector will lead to much higher allocations which the defence services may not be able to absorb." PRS adds that 3% in 2025-26 would mean Rs 10.7 lakh crore, or 21% of central spending. PRS also notes that "in 2023-24 and 2024-25, the allocation for the capital budget of the armed forces has been in line with their projections." Source: https://prsindia.org/files/budget/budget_parliament/2025/DFG_Analysis_2025-26_Defence.pdf. The Ministry contradicts itself: in its 15th FC memo it said the shortfalls caused "serious capability gaps". Both statements are on the record.
verdicts.innocentReading: GDP grew faster than the defence budget: defence grew 9% a year against 10% for total central spending between 2013-14 and 2025-26. On top of that, pay and pension take about 50% of the budget, and the Ministry says it could not absorb a 3% allocation. Together these explain the falling ratio without any deliberate starving of the services. The 3% figure is a legislative committee recommendation, and the services' projections are requests, not audited capability needs.
verdicts.reason: The narrative stands as "contested". Every number checks against the opened PDFs: SC 2018 "about 3% of GDP"; "1.9% of its GDP" for 2025-26; 17% in 2014-15 to 13% in 2025-26; capital outlay "less than 30%" (28% in 2025-26); Rs 9.01 vs 17.46 lakh crore; SIPRI 5th, $86.1bn, 2.3%, global 2.5%. It is a value question, and the record does not dress it up as fact. But the strongestCounter contains a false statement and leaves out the strongest counter in its own source. "The 3% target has no peer basis" is wrong. In SIPRI Table 1, the US (3.4), Poland (4.2) and four others are above 3%, and NATO's Hague Summit Declaration of 25 June 2025 commits allies to 3.5% of GDP on core defence by 2035 (https://www.nato.int/en/about-us/official-texts-and-resources/official-texts/2025/06/25/the-hague-summit-declaration). Meanwhile the MoD's own "may not be able to absorb" statement, the actual government response, is left out. These are field errors to fix, not a refutation of the claim. The tier is analytic: the numbers it rests on are documented, but the calibration is our own inference.
verdicts.corrections: 1. strongestCounter: delete "the 3% target has no peer basis". Replace it with the MoD's statement quoted from PRS ("spending 3% ... may not be able to absorb"; 3% = Rs 10.7 lakh crore = 21% of central spending), plus PRS's note that capital allocations matched projections in 2023-24 and 2024-25. 2. strongestCounter: change "near the 2.5% world average" to "below the 2.5% global military burden (world spending/world GDP); SIPRI's country averages are 1.9% for countries not in conflict and 4.4% for countries in conflict". Label "median of the fifteen largest" as our own computation from SIPRI Table 1. 3. strongestCase: change "the Ministry reports committed-liability shortfalls" to "the Standing Committee on Defence (2019) flagged shortfalls on committed liabilities; the Ministry told the 15th FC that shortfalls caused 'serious capability gaps'". Keep the 9.01 vs 17.46 lakh crore figures (48% shortfall). 4. strongestCase: add the pro-3% peer facts that the counter currently denies, citing SIPRI Table 1 and NATO's Hague declaration: Pakistan 2.7%, South Korea 2.6%, US 3.4%, and NATO's 3.5% core target from 2025. 5. Rename "denominator question" to "definition question". State that PRS's 1.9% (about 1.4% without pension) is the MoD budget, while SIPRI's 2.3% includes paramilitary forces. 6. Add the UPA control: capital share was 32% in 2013-14; SIPRI had India at 2.5% in 2015; the gap to 3% predates 2014. 7. whatWouldChangeThis: note that the Ministry already claims capability gaps in its 15th FC memo, so the deciding test is an independent CAG or SC capability audit, not a first claim of a gap.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, put as actor/did/thing/when: the MoD's 2025-26 BE demand puts about half of its ₹6,81,210 crore on salaries plus pensions. A second figure covers 2022-23 revenue expenditure. The years line up and the record labels each figure with its own year. PRS (Feb 4, 2025) says: "Salaries and pension account for 50% of the estimated spending on defence in 2025-26." It also says "In 2025-26, 24% of the total defence budget is estimated to be spent on pension." ORF IB 567 (2023-08-16) says: "In 2022-23, P&A and Pension will add up to INR 287,040 crore, or 79 percent of the MoD's total revenue expenditure." The 79% is a share of revenue expenditure in a different year, not a share of the total demand. The record sets it beside the 2025-26 shares in strongestCase. It is labelled correctly, but the two figures should not be read as the same measure. No actor-tenure question arises because the claim names no person or office.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is the right one: Ministry of Defence, total allocation (Table 2, PRS). Two definitional caveats are missing from the record. (1) PRS's "Salaries" line "include[s] pay and allowances of the armed forces, auxiliary forces, civilians, research and development, and salary expenditure of the civil estimates". It is not just soldiers' pay, and PRS adds that it "could be an underestimate" because the Rashtriya Rifles, NCC and Agnipath revenue lines have no breakup. (2) The pension line covers 32,94,181 pensioners. ORF counts 26,79,645 military pensioners or dependents and 6,14,536 defence civilians. strongestCounter's "contracts with 26.8 lakh people" counts only the military share and understates the pension base.
verdicts.baseRate: The property "about half the defence budget goes to pay and pensions" does not set India apart. Personnel-heavy budgets are the norm among large conscript or volunteer land armies. Under NATO's own definition, which includes pensions, many members put 40-60% of defence spending into personnel, which is why the alliance had to set an equipment floor of at least 20%. I did not re-fetch that peer figure here, so the claim cannot rest on it. On symmetry with UPA-II: PRS says capital outlay was 32% of the budget in 2013-14 and below 30% from 2014-15 to 2024-25. Pension grew 11% a year from 2013-14 to 2025-26 against 9% for the total. Part of that rise comes from OROP (2015) and the 7th CPC (2016), both NDA-era policy choices. So the description holds under either government. What changed after 2014 is the trend, not the type of budget.
verdicts.denialFound: No MoD denial of the shares was found; I did not ask MoD. PRS itself records the counterpoint the claim leaves out: "Allocation for capital acquisition has improved in recent years". It also shows capital outlay rising 13% to ₹1,92,388 crore (2025-26 BE) from ₹1,70,485 crore (2024-25 RE). ORF, the scheme's defenders, call the budget "already personnel-heavy" and say it "would have become unsustainable to fund essential future procurement". That is a forward warning, not a finding that modernisation is starved today. The Ministry's own position, quoted by PRS, is that funding shortfalls have caused "serious capability gaps". That supports pressure on the capital budget, not "nothing".
verdicts.innocentReading: Pensions and pay are deferred and current wages owed to about 14 lakh serving personnel and about 33 lakh military and civilian pensioners. The pension share rose after OROP (2015) and the 7th CPC (2016), both policy decisions about people. Defence budgets with large standing armies are personnel-heavy everywhere. Meanwhile capital outlay is still 28% of the demand (₹1.92 lakh crore) and growing in rupee terms.
verdicts.reason: Both sources confirm the descriptive core (PRS: salaries and pensions 50%, pensions 24%; ORF: pensions +163% against MoD +107%, and P&A plus pension 79% of revenue in 2022-23). But the narrative as stored in literature.json reads "eaten by pensions and pay, leaving nothing for modernisation" and is marked "well-supported". The same PRS document contradicts the second clause. Capital outlay is ₹1,92,388 crore, 28% of the 2025-26 BE and up 13%, and PRS says capital acquisition allocation "has improved in recent years". The 48% shortfall against the 2021-26 projection is evidence that modernisation is underfunded, not that it gets nothing. A single "well-supported" status on the full sentence overstates the evidence. The defensible statement is narrower: pay and pensions take about half the demand, and pensions grew faster than the total.
verdicts.corrections:
Edit narratives entry 6 (line ~2067) in /home/user/india-corporate-intelligence/research/raw/force/literature.json:
(1) Change status from "well-supported" to "partly supported". The pay-and-pension half is supported; "leaving nothing for modernisation" is contradicted by PRS Table 2 (capital outlay ₹1,92,388 crore, 28%, +13% RE→BE).
(2) Add to strongestCounter: "Capital outlay ₹1,92,388 crore = 28% of 2025-26 BE, up 13% over 2024-25 RE; PRS: 'Allocation for capital acquisition has improved in recent years'."
(3) Fix "contracts with 26.8 lakh people" to "about 32.9 lakh pensioners (26.8 lakh military or dependents, 6.1 lakh defence civilians, ORF as of 2021-04-01)".
(4) Note in strongestCase that PRS's 'salaries' line includes civilians, R&D and civil-estimate salaries, and that the 79% is a share of 2022-23 revenue expenditure, not of the total demand.
(5) Add PRS's own growth comparison (pension 11% a year against 9% for the total, 2013-14→2025-26) and the UPA-II baseline (capital 32% in 2013-14) as the symmetry line.
(6) Tier the underlying figures as reported (PRS/ORF transcription of budget documents). Upgrade to documented once the pay-pensions domain reproduces them from the Defence Pensions and Defence Services demand PDFs.

verdicts.dateTest: Pass. Restated: "The Union government (MoD, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh) adopted Agnipath for cost reasons while presenting it as reform, June 2022." The scheme was announced 14 June 2022, during Rajnath Singh's tenure as Defence Minister (2019 to present). The DPG brief is dated "June 24, 2022" (confirmed on the page). The ORF brief shows "Published on Aug 16, 2023" (confirmed; it is an update of a 2022 version). The ORF footnotes cite the PIB press briefing and the DMA media conference of June 2022. Nothing is out of sequence.
verdicts.identityTest: Fails on the key point. The narrative names the "proponents" (ORF authors Laxman Kumar Behera and Vinay Kaushal, who are outside analysts) as the people who "openly stated" the cost motive. The party that could have disguised it is a different actor: the government, MoD and DMA. That actor's position runs the other way. The ORF brief itself says: "While unveiling the Agnipath scheme, the government denied any financial motive behind the radical change in recruitment policy. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh emphasised: 'We never see the army from the point of view of savings.'" It also says: "Though the official explanation for the scheme is to make the forces younger and more tech-savvy, it is equally driven by a strong financial motive." The DPG brief says: "The government and the military are silent on the issue of manpower savings that would accrue due to the Agnipath scheme. However, it is apparent that the rising pay and pension budget has been a key factor." Think-tank authors being open about the motive does not show the government was.
verdicts.baseRate: Not measured. Governments that restructure military manpower (shorter terms, fewer pensions) usually present the change publicly as a capability or youth-profile reform, while the fiscal case comes from analysts and budget documents. So a gap between the official framing and the cost motive is probably common, which makes "disguised" a weak signal of deliberate deception in itself. The same lens applied to India's own history: the Balaram committee (1985) and the colour-service proposals of the early 1990s openly argued cost-effectiveness, and later proposals discussed savings openly. I found no case-set to compute a fraction.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes: the government denied the financial motive, and both cited sources record it. (1) Rajnath Singh, June 2022 PIB press briefing, quoted in ORF IB 567 (https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-case-for-agnipath): "We never see the army from the point of view of savings." (2) The Wire, "Why Is the Military Disowning Agnipath's Pension Saving Element?" (https://thewire.in/security/agnipath-scheme-pension-savings-military-denial) reports that senior officers of all three services and the DMA under Lt Gen Anil Puri declared pension savings were "most definitely" not a consideration. Per the search-result summary, Puri also said his analysis had "no financial chapter". (3) DPG (https://www.delhipolicygroup.org/publication/policy-briefs/the-agnipath-scheme-analysis-and-a-way-forward.html) says "the government and the military are silent on the issue of manpower savings."
verdicts.innocentReading: Agnipath really does serve both aims, and ORF's own words are "equally driven". The youth-profile aim (average age from 32 to 24–26, in line with peer armies) is real. On ORF's arithmetic the pension savings only arrive after 2044 ("there will be no savings in the near to medium term"), so leading with youth and capability is a defensible description of the near-term effect, not necessarily a cover story. A government may also avoid citing pension savings for political reasons, because of protests and veterans' sensitivity, without the reform being a pretext.
verdicts.reason: The narrative's verdict that "'disguised' fails" is contradicted by both of its own sources. The cost motive is well supported: ORF computes it and DPG calls it "apparent". But the government and military officially denied it (Rajnath Singh: "We never see the army from the point of view of savings"; the DMA and service officers said savings were "most definitely" not a consideration). DPG records them as "silent" on savings. The narrative's own whatWouldChangeThis says the verdict "would move only if MoD disavowed the fiscal rationale", and the MoD did disavow it in June 2022, as the cited ORF brief reports. So the record supports this: an undisclosed or denied co-motive alongside a real youth-profile reform. "Disguised" is partly supported as a documented gap between the official framing and the analysis on both sides. "Cost-cutting measure disguised as reform" still overstates it, because the reform aim is real and the savings are long-dated. The status should be "contested", not a clean "motive well-supported; 'disguised' fails."
verdicts.corrections:
narratives[7] (the Agnipath entry; it is labelled narrative:7 in the task):
(a) status: change "well-supported" to "contested", or "partly supported": the cost motive is well supported as a co-driver, the "disguised" framing is partly supported, and the "merely cost-cutting" reading is unsupported.
(b) strongestCounter: delete "The financial motive is not disguised — it is published by the proponents". Replace it with: "The reform aim is real (MoD's goal of cutting average age from 32 to 24–26); ORF finds no pension savings before 2044, so the near-term rationale is youth profile, not cost."
(c) strongestCase: add the official denial: "ORF itself records that 'the government denied any financial motive' (Rajnath Singh: 'We never see the army from the point of view of savings'); DPG: 'The government and the military are silent on the issue of manpower savings… it is apparent that the rising pay and pension budget has been a key factor.'"
(d) whatWouldChangeThis: its stated trigger (MoD disavowing the fiscal rationale) already happened in June 2022. Rewrite it as: "Up: an MoD or DMA document (cabinet note, DMA study, Standing Committee answer) that names pension savings as an objective. Down: evidence that the 2020–21 proposal, mooted under CDS Bipin Rawat, was framed only on youth profile."
(e) Add a contra/source: The Wire, https://thewire.in/security/agnipath-scheme-pension-savings-military-denial.
(f) Do not call the ORF authors "proponents" in a sense that stands in for the government; label them "independent proponents (ORF)".
(g) Edge label at line 1562 ("by its proponents' own arithmetic") is fine as written.

verdicts.dateTest: The narrative joins figures from two different years and two documents. 155 per lakh is the actual strength on 2023-01-01. The source is the PRS DFG 2025-26 Home Affairs PDF, p.~2: "As of January 2023, India has 155 police personnel for every one lakh people." Its Annexure Table 15 also gives "India 155" and cites BPR&D DoPO, March 2024. The 222 figure comes from PRS 2017, which sets it against January 2016 figures (sanctioned 181, actual 137): "Note that the United Nations recommended standard is 222 police per lakh persons." The 2025 PDF does not mention 222 at all. So the pairing 155 vs 222 is our own conjunction, or a press one (Business Standard on X, 2025, uses 154.84 vs 222). No single opened source makes it. The two numbers are compatible in kind (actual strength against a claimed norm), so the date mismatch does not distort anything. It should still be recorded as a cross-document pairing.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match what the sources name. "India" is the all-India actual police per lakh in BPR&D Data on Police Organisations as on 2023-01-01, as transcribed by PRS. That is the state police total, which is the figure the 222 comparison is usually made against. "UN" is a pure attribution. PRS 2017 calls it the "United Nations recommended standard". It does not cite a UN document: footnotes [8] and [33] point to BPR&D DoPO 2016 and to BPR&D's "National Requirement of Manpower for 8-hour Shifts in Police Stations" (August 2014). No UN resolution, UNODC standard or UNPOL manual was found. Africa Check (via polity.org.za, 2019-07-02) traces the equivalent 1:450 ratio (= 222 per lakh) to US policing of occupied Germany in 1945. It reports "The UN did not respond to our queries about if they have any ratio", and Mark Shaw (GI-TOC) says such norms "are not there" in UN standards.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not discriminating at the national level, and it is not partisan. From PRS Table 15 (2023-01-01), 20 of 36 states and UTs are below 222. Every large state except Punjab (241) is below it: Bihar 81, WB 101, Rajasthan 118, MP 121, Odisha 121, Gujarat 124, UP 135, Maharashtra 137, Karnataka 151, Kerala 151, Jharkhand 158, TN 160, Telangana 163, AP 166. The states above 222 are mostly small, North-Eastern, border, or UTs. On the symmetry control, low ratios appear in BJP-run states (Gujarat, UP, MP), opposition-run ones (WB, Kerala, TN, Telangana) and states under mixed control in January 2023 (Bihar, Odisha, Rajasthan, Karnataka). The lens gives the same picture whichever party governs, so it says nothing about party. The documented shortfall is against India's own sanctioned strength: 181 vs 137 in 2016 per PRS 2017, about 196 vs 155 in 2023 per Business Standard. The 222 norm is not the documented benchmark.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial from a party to the claim was found. The UN has not been recorded confirming or denying the 222/1:450 norm: Africa Check asked, and "The UN did not respond to our queries about if they have any ratio" (https://www.polity.org.za/article/south-african-police-minister-cites-dubious-un-standard-as-he-calls-for-60-000-more-officers-2019-07-02). Africa Check's follow-up is headlined "Still no UN recommended police-to-population ratio" (https://africacheck.org/fact-checks/spotchecks/still-no-un-recommended-police-population-ratio-ghost-statistic-cited-again). That page returned 403 here and was not opened. MHA was not asked by us. A 2021 Rajya Sabha unstarred answer by MoS G. Kishan Reddy gave sanctioned 195.39 and actual 155.78 per lakh in reply to a question that cited UN recommendations; that answer was not opened here.
verdicts.innocentReading: 155 per lakh is a real, documented low ratio by international comparison, and vacancies against India's own sanctioned norms are real. But "222" is a ghost statistic that Indian policy writing (PRS 2017, the Standing Committee, the press) has repeated as a UN standard without a UN instrument behind it. Low ratios in large, populous states may also reflect how much a state budget can pay for, and the federal division of policing (a State List subject). They do not by themselves show that India is "dangerously" under-policed. No Indian elasticity linking police numbers to crime was opened, and Chalfin & McCrary's estimate is for US cities only.
verdicts.reason: The calibrated verdict holds. The 155 figure is quoted verbatim from the 2025 PRS PDF and its Table 15. The 222 figure is quoted verbatim from PRS 2017 as a "United Nations recommended standard", but the footnotes point to BPR&D, not to a UN document. Africa Check reports that the UN did not answer when asked about any such ratio, and it traces 1:450 to occupied Germany in 1945. Neither lens refutes the record. It is not debunked because there is no explicit UN denial on file, but it cannot be upgraded. "Dangerously" is a normative word with no evidence behind it. One wording fix is needed: "unsourced" overstates the gap, since PRS does footnote the figure (to BPR&D), just not to the UN. The narrative is our own calibration, so its tier stays analytic.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Change "222 unsourced" to "222 attributed to the UN by PRS 2017 (footnotes [8], [33]: BPR&D DoPO 2016 and BPR&D 'National Requirement of Manpower for 8-hour Shifts', Aug 2014); no UN instrument located". 2) In force:lit-prs-police-reforms-2017 'Does not establish', replace "PRS cites it as an international guideline without a UN instrument" with "PRS calls it the 'United Nations recommended standard' and footnotes BPR&D documents, not a UN document". 3) In whatWouldChangeThis, the "Down" evidence was "not opened here" and is now opened: add the src ["Africa Check via Polity, 2019-07-02 — 'South African police minister cites dubious UN standard'", "https://www.polity.org.za/article/south-african-police-minister-cites-dubious-un-standard-as-he-calls-for-60-000-more-officers-2019-07-02"] as the strongestCounter source. It quotes "The UN did not respond to our queries about if they have any ratio" and traces 1:450 to occupied Germany in 1945. 4) Note in strongestCase that 155 (2023, PRS 2025) and 222 (PRS 2017) come from different documents. PRS 2025 does not mention 222. 5) Add the state base rate to strongestCounter: 20 of 36 states/UTs are below 222, including every large state except Punjab, in both BJP-run and opposition-run states. 6) Drop or flag "dangerously" as an unevidenced normative claim. 7) Optional upgradeIf for the 155 figure: open the 2021 Rajya Sabha unstarred answer (actual 155.78, sanctioned 195.39) or BPR&D DoPO 2023 directly, which would make 155 documented rather than reported.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: state and Union governments did not implement the seven Prakash Singh directives, which were issued 2006-09-22 with a compliance deadline of 2006-12-31, between 2006 and now. The judgment (Indian Kanoon 1090328) confirms the date and the deadline: "The aforesaid directions shall be complied with ... on or before 31st December, 2006". The judgment cannot speak to implementation that came later. The two SPIR sources are dated 2018 and 2019 and describe data up to 2016–17. The claim is in the present tense as of 2026 but rests on evidence that is 7–9 years old. Newer measurements exist (CHRI Sept 2021; Bar & Bench 2026-09-11) and the file did not open them. The dates line up, but the evidence is stale for a present-tense statement.
verdicts.identityTest: The case is identified correctly: Prakash Singh & Ors v Union of India, WP(C) 310/1996, judgment of 22 Sep 2006, with its seven directives (SSC, DGP selection and tenure, two-year tenure for IG and field officers, separating investigation from law and order, PEB, PCA, NSC). The SPIR 2018 lists the same seven. One problem: the narrative's strongestCase cites "PRS 2017" on ministerial use of police, but no PRS URL is in srcs, so that part of the case is unsourced in this record. Also, Common Cause, which wrote both SPIR reports, is a co-petitioner in the case. SPIR 2018 says: "Prakash Singh case, in which Common Cause was a co-petitioner". So the 'independent' corroboration comes from a party to the case.
verdicts.baseRate: Non-compliance is close to universal. CHRI (Sept 2021) found "NO STATE COMPLIANT" on the SSC directive: 26 of 28 states non-compliant and 1 partially compliant. On PEBs only 2 of 27 fully comply (Arunachal, Karnataka) and 5 partially. But formal adoption is also close to universal: "27 out of 28 states have constituted an SSC, either through Police Acts or government orders", and "all states, except Telangana, have constituted Police Establishment Boards on paper". So the accurate reading is that states adopted the structures on paper but almost none comply in substance. A flat "not implemented" is wrong on the formal side. Because non-compliance is above 80% across states, it tells you nothing about any one party or government. The SPIR evidence is symmetric: the most compliant states are HP, Uttarakhand and Kerala, which have had different ruling parties. High premature transfers occur in Haryana and UP, and election-year spikes appear in BJP-run Gujarat and Chhattisgarh as well as Jharkhand. The narrative does not attribute non-compliance to one party, so the symmetry control passes.
verdicts.denialFound: The record has no response field. The states' position is on record but not in the file. SPIR 2019 says: "five States—Punjab, Haryana, West Bengal, Kerala and Bihar—had moved the Apex Court seeking modification of the above directive regarding minimum tenure. These pleas, however, were dismissed". States also argue that police is a state subject and that they have enacted Police Acts: SPIR 2018 counts 13 Acts and later commentary counts about 17. Bar & Bench (Fahas Abdulla, 2026-09-11, https://www.barandbench.com/columns/twenty-years-of-prakash-singh-when-does-non-compliance-become-contempt) summarises three recurring state defences and concludes "States and UTs have only been partially compliant". No direct comment from the Union or state governments was sought by this file (not asked).
verdicts.innocentReading: The boring explanation is partial, formal compliance. Most states legislated or issued government orders setting up the SSC, PEB and PCA, but designed them to keep executive control (no Leader of Opposition, government-nominated members, recommendations that are not binding). That is non-compliance in substance, not a refusal to implement at all. The tenure directive also had a measurable effect. SPIR 2019, one of the file's own sources, says premature SSP/DIG transfers fell "from 37 percent in 2007 to 13 percent in 2016 ... The judgment, therefore, appears to have a tangible impact". A claim that the directives were "not implemented" contradicts this.
verdicts.reason: Refuted as worded. The cited sources do not say the directives "have not been implemented". SPIR 2018 says states are "not implementing the Apex Court's directives fully and unequivocally", that 13 states passed Police Acts, that the NSC was formed in 2017, and that HP, Uttarakhand and Kerala show relatively better compliance. SPIR 2019 says the tenure directive "appears to have a tangible impact". CHRI 2021 shows that SSCs and PEBs were set up on paper in 27 of 28 states while almost none comply in substance. So the defensible claim is "no state fully complies; most formally adopted the structures in diluted form". The summary also calls the claim "unmeasured" when a state-by-state measurement (CHRI 2021) exists. Both main sources are by Common Cause, a co-petitioner, so this should sit at reported, not documented. A primary record (SC compliance affidavits, the Justice Thomas Committee report) would be needed to upgrade it.
verdicts.corrections: 1. claim: change to "No state fully complies with the SC's 2006 Prakash Singh directives. Most constituted SSCs and PEBs on paper (27/28 SSCs per CHRI 2021) in diluted form, and substantive compliance is rare." 2. Add CHRI, "Government Compliance with SC Directives on Police Reforms: An Assessment" (Sept 2021), https://www.humanrightsinitiative.org/download/1632218542Government%20Compliance%20with%20SC%20Directives%20On%20Police%20Reforms%20An%20Assessment.pdf, to srcs. Then rewrite whatWouldChangeThis, because the compliance table it asks for already exists, and drop "unmeasured" from the summary text. 3. strongestCase: either add the PRS 2017 URL to srcs or remove the PRS sentence. 4. strongestCounter: quote SPIR 2019 directly ("from 37 percent in 2007 to 13 percent in 2016 ... appears to have a tangible impact") and the 2017 NSC formation from SPIR 2018. 5. Note that Common Cause, the SPIR author, is a co-petitioner in the case. 6. Set the tier to reported, with upgradeIf: SC compliance affidavits or the Justice K.T. Thomas Committee report (2010) opened. 7. Add an asOf caveat: the SPIR data runs to 2016–17 and the CHRI data to 2021. 8. Add a response line with the states' recorded positions (the modification pleas dismissed by the SC, the police-as-state-subject argument, enacted Police Acts), and record that no comment was sought.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MoD awarded Mahindra Defence Systems Ltd a contract for 14 IADS worth Rs 1,349.95 crore on 27 Aug 2021. The cited Mahindra release is datelined "Delhi, August 27, 2021". PIB PRID 1749636 says the contract was concluded "in New Delhi on August 27, 2021". The two dates match. MDS was a Mahindra subsidiary at that time, so there is no ownership-window problem. The file's note that the award came about 17 months before M&M's bond purchase of 27 Jan 2023 is correct arithmetic. Because the award came first, it cannot be a reward for that purchase.
verdicts.identityTest: Both sources name the same entity. The Mahindra release names "Mahindra Defence Systems Limited (MDS)". PIB says "Ministry of Defence (MoD) has concluded a contract with Mahindra Defence Systems Limited for procurement of 14 Integrated Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) Defence Suites (IADS) at a cost of Rs 1,349.95 crore". The awarder (MoD), winner (MDS, the subsidiary and not parent M&M), unit count (14), amount (Rs 1,349.95 cr) and buyer service (Indian Navy) all match. The node force:mahindra-defence-systems has to stay separate from the M&M bond-buyer node. Linking the two requires an `own` edge, not a merged node.
verdicts.baseRate: MoD awards contracts to licensed private Indian vendors all the time, and many of them are Buy and Make (Indian) or Make awards that companies and PIB announce. Getting an MoD order does not set a vendor apart, and the edge does not claim it does. On symmetry: no DPSU competitor in the IADS tender is named in either source. The SPEC control (private vendor beside the DPSU in the same category and years, e.g. BEL in naval sonar and ASW) has not been run for this line and should be recorded as not run, not presumed.
verdicts.denialFound: None needed, and none found (not asked). This is a plain award fact confirmed by the awarder (PIB) and by the winner. Neither party disputes it.
verdicts.innocentReading: The ordinary explanation is a routine indigenous procurement. PIB says it was under the 'Buy and Make (Indian)' category, and Mahindra says it was an open tender among Indian companies, with systems tested in sea trials and the winner chosen on the commercial bid. The award came about 17 months before the parent's Rs 25 cr bond purchase, so the edge supports no quid-pro-quo reading on its own.
verdicts.reason: The claim is not refuted. Both the company release and the Government of India primary record (PIB PRID 1749636, 27 Aug 2021) state the same awarder, winner, unit count, amount and date. With a PIB release in hand, the contract's tier rule makes this `documented`; the current `reported` label rests only on the self-interested company release. The claim names no individual, gives no operational or deployment detail, and concerns a procurement that was publicly announced, so none of the refusals apply.
verdicts.corrections: 1. tier: change "reported" to "documented". 2. srcs: add ["PIB (MoD) - Boost to 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' in defence: contract with Mahindra Defence Systems for 14 IADS, Rs 1,349.95 crore (27 Aug 2021)", "https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleseDetailm.aspx?PRID=1749636"]. 3. text: drop "(company release)" or change it to "(PIB; company release)". 4. d: replace "Category: Integrated Anti-Submarine Warfare Defence Suite (shipborne)" with "Procurement category: Buy and Make (Indian) (PIB); item: Integrated ASW Defence Suite, 14 units for Indian Navy warships". Keep the AoN/DAC void. 5. Line 917 and the narrative strongestCase (around line 3904): add the PIB source and change [reported] to [documented]. 6. symmetryCheck: record that the private-vendor-beside-DPSU control was not run for the IADS tender. 7. Keep MDS (subsidiary) and M&M (bond buyer) as separate nodes, joined by an explicit `own` edge with its source.

verdicts.dateTest: Stated as an actor, an action, an object and a time: three donors (Megha Engineering, Mahindra & Mahindra, Cyient) bought bonds encashed by the BJP and by other parties, 12 Apr 2019 to 15 Feb 2024 (the ADR-matched SBI disclosure released by ECI on 21 Mar 2024). The figures and the window match. The claim makes no award-after-bond timing assertion, so the date test does not bind on it. The sibling claim c022 shows that the one documented MoD award (Mahindra Defence, 27 Aug 2021) predates the Mahindra bond (27 Jan 2023). The 46.1% BJP share covers only the matched April 2019 to February 2024 set. Over the whole scheme (2018 to 2024) the share was about 50% (Rs 8,252 cr of Rs 16,492 cr, per Scroll). The label should keep the window explicit.
verdicts.identityTest: Partial pass. The donor names match the ADR rows exactly: MEGHA ENGINEERING & INFRASTRUCTURES LIMITED / ...LI MITED / ...LTD (sno 800-811, together Rs 966 cr), MAHINDRA & MAHINDRA LTD (sno 774, Rs 25 cr BJP) and CYIENT LIMITED (sno 309, Rs 10 cr BJP). The identity problem is the category, not the names. Megha is 96.5% of the "defence-linked" pool (966 of 1,001), and the file's own Megha claims say: "its strategic Zojila tunnel contract (2020) was awarded by NHIDCL, not by the Ministry of Defence, and no MoD award to MEIL is in this file; it is included because the brief names it". The Mahindra bond was bought by the listed parent, while the MoD contract is with the subsidiary Mahindra Defence Systems. The file does not size Cyient's defence share ("the defence share of the donor entity's business was not" measured). So "defence-linked donors' mix" is in substance Megha's mix, and Megha's defence link is not documented in the file.
verdicts.baseRate:
I re-parsed all 56 ADR donor-alphabetical pages myself: 1,655 rows summing to Rs 12,145.88 cr. The BJP gets Rs 5,594.20 cr (46.06%). Megha's split is BJP 584, BRS 195, DMK 85, YSRCP 37, TDP 28, INC 18, JD(U) 10, JD(S) 5, Janasena 4, total 966. The BJP took 619 of the three donors' 1,001 (61.8%). My own name normalisation gives 362 of 1,244 donors (29.1%) giving only to the BJP, matching the file's 372/1,280. So the arithmetic holds. The comparison does not discriminate:
(a) Among donors of Rs 10 cr or more, the value-weighted BJP share is 47.6%, and 73.7% (file) / ~74% (mine) gave to the BJP at least once. All three "defence-linked" donors (3/3) gave to the BJP, which is the expected result at that base rate. Two of three gave only to the BJP, against 38.4%; with n=3 that carries no signal.
(b) Among donors of Rs 100 cr or more, Megha's 60.5% to the BJP sits mid-pack. Higher shares: Qwik Supply 91.5%, Madanlal 94.6%, Bharti Airtel 100%, DLF Commercial 100%, Birla Carbon 100%, Keventer 74.1%, Torrent Power 71.4%. Lower shares: Future Gaming 8.3%, Haldia 21.5%, Essel 22.3%, Jindal Steel & Power 2.4%.
(c) Infrastructure contractors with no defence label show the same or a higher BJP share: NCC 100%, Navayuga Engineering 100%, APCO Infratech 100%, KEC 100%, Kalpataru 100%. Navayuga's strategic road-tunnel work is the same kind of NHIDCL work as Megha's Zojila, yet the "defence or strategic-works" rule was not applied to it. So the inclusion rule was not applied the same way to every donor.
(d) The headline sets value shares (61.8%, 46.1%) beside a donor-count share (29.1%). These are different units.
verdicts.denialFound: Party level: Amit Shah (15 Mar 2024) said electoral bonds are not black money and that the BJP got about Rs 6,000 cr with 303 MPs while other parties got Rs 14,000 cr (Tribune, https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/bonds-not-black-money-whats-the-ruckus-all-about-asks-shah-601010). Scroll fact-checked this as an understatement: the BJP actually received Rs 8,252 cr of Rs 16,492 cr (https://scroll.in/article/1065281/home-minister-amit-shah-cited-wrong-data-to-underplay-bjps-share-of-electoral-bonds). Donor level: no statement found from Megha, Mahindra or Cyient about these specific bonds, and the file records no attempt to ask them.
verdicts.innocentReading: Large infrastructure and engineering firms that hold contracts from both the Union government and state governments buy bonds for the party in power at the Centre and for the parties ruling the states where they work. Megha's spread fits this: BRS in Telangana, YSRCP and TDP in Andhra Pradesh, DMK in Tamil Nadu, JD(S) in Karnataka. Its above-average BJP share is typical for donors of Rs 100 cr or more, and lower than that of many infrastructure contractors with no defence line. The 61.8% is one irrigation and power contractor's mix plus Rs 35 cr from two listed conglomerates. It says nothing about defence procurement.
verdicts.reason: The numbers are correct and documented. I confirmed them against all 56 ADR pages: 61.8% (619/1,001), 46.06% (5,594.20/12,145.88) and 29.1% donor-only. The headline contrast does not survive, for three reasons. First, the "defence-linked" pool is 96.5% Megha, which the file itself says has no MoD award and was "included because the brief names it". Second, the right comparator, donors of similar size (≥Rs 10 cr: 47.6% value-weighted BJP, 74% gave to the BJP at least once), and infrastructure contractors with no defence label (NCC, Navayuga, APCO, KEC, Kalpataru, all 100% BJP) give the same or a higher reading. So the lens does not separate defence from non-defence donors. Third, the label mixes value shares with a donor-count share. As written, the edge implies a defence-specific BJP tilt that the controls dissolve. It survives only if rewritten as a plain named-donor comparison with the like-for-like control beside it. analytic is the right tier for that rewrite. The current wording should not ship.
verdicts.corrections:
1) text/lab: replace "Defence-linked donors' bond mix (61.8% BJP)" with "Megha Engineering, Mahindra & Mahindra and Cyient: 61.8% of Rs 1,001 cr to the BJP (Megha alone is Rs 966 cr, 60.5% BJP), against 47.6% for all donors of Rs 10 cr or more and 46.1% for all matched bonds". Drop "29.1% of donors BJP-only" from the headline, or pair it with the like-for-like count (2 of 3 BJP-only vs 38.4% among donors of Rs 10 cr or more; 3 of 3 gave to the BJP at least once vs 73.7%).
2) d: state that Megha is 96.5% of the pool and that its only "strategic" work in the file is an NHIDCL (MoRTH) award with no MoD award. State that the Mahindra bond was bought by the parent, not the MoD-contracted subsidiary. Add the infrastructure control: NCC 60/60, Navayuga 55/55, APCO 30/30, KEC 11/11, Kalpataru 25.5/25.5 to the BJP, and Jindal Steel & Power 3/123.
3) baseRates: add "value-weighted BJP share, donors ≥ Rs 10 cr: 47.6% (215–224 donors)", and replace the 2/3 row with 3/3 gave-at-least-once vs 165/224.
4) d: note the window (matched set Apr 2019–Feb 2024). The whole-scheme BJP share is about 50% (Rs 8,252 cr of Rs 16,492 cr).
5) Add a line on the party's public answer (Shah, 15 Mar 2024) and record "donors not asked".
6) innocentReading: add "Megha's BJP share is mid-pack among donors ≥ Rs 100 cr and below that of non-defence infrastructure contractors".

verdicts.dateTest: Written out, the claim says MoD awarded Mahindra Defence Systems Ltd the IADS contract (Rs 1,349.95 cr, 14 systems) on 2021-08-27, and Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd bought 25 bonds of Rs 1 cr each, all to the BJP, on 2023-01-27. Both dates are confirmed. The Mahindra release says: "Delhi, August 27, 2021 - The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has awarded a major contract to Mahindra Defence Systems Limited (MDS) worth Rs.1349.95 Cr". On MyNeta every row reads "27/Jan/2023 | BHARATIYA JANATA PARTY", encashed between 30 Jan and 07 Feb 2023. The claim leaves the later period unsearched, and that is where it fails. On 27 Mar 2025, 26 months after the purchase, MoD signed a contract with Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd itself, alongside Force Motors, for about 5,000 Light Vehicles (M&M about 1,986). Devdiscourse, reporting the PIB release, says: "The contracts, totalling approximately ₹2,500 crore, were signed with three Indian companies: Armoured Vehicle Nigam Limited (AVNL), Force Motors Ltd, and Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd." AVNL's NAMIS share was Rs 1,801.34 cr, which leaves about Rs 700 cr for the light vehicles. One further order, the 1,300 LSVs (Rs 1,056 cr, signed March 2021), also came before the bond. So the post-bond order exists. The test comes out mixed and must not be presented as a pass.
verdicts.identityTest: The IADS award went to Mahindra Defence Systems Ltd, a subsidiary. The bond buyer was MAHINDRA & MAHINDRA LTD, the listed parent. The claim's s=co:mahindra-mahindra is correct for the bond. However, the entity record force:mahindra-defence-systems says "MoD contracts are with this subsidiary, not with the listed parent", and that is false: the 27 Mar 2025 PIB-reported contract names Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd, the same legal entity that bought the bonds. That matters more than the subsidiary award, because no subsidiary-to-parent step is needed. A further check is still needed: whether MDSL had merged into M&M or been restructured by then.
verdicts.baseRate: The sample is three bond donors with a defence line. The control fails as a control. Force Motors, the co-winner of the same 27 Mar 2025 contract (2,978 Gurkha LSVs), also bought BJP-only bonds: Rs 6.35 cr, purchased 2019-05-06 and 2023-10-11, according to this same file's void entry. So both private winners of that award had bought BJP bonds. The non-buying winner was a DPSU (AVNL). A BJP-only donor pattern describes 29.1% of all donors, and orders were awarded to both buyers through a Buy (IDDM) competitive route. Nothing here separates buyers from non-buyers. The killIf test (comparing award rates of non-buying vendors such as L&T, Tata and Bharat Forge) has not been run.
verdicts.denialFound: None found from Mahindra & Mahindra on its Rs 25 cr purchase. Nothing shows the company was asked. The only response on record is the BJP's general one, which applies to the whole scheme and not to Mahindra: spokesperson Zafar Islam said "it is very unfair to cast any quid-pro-quo doubts here". The Supreme Court struck the scheme down for opacity and made no quid-pro-quo finding.
verdicts.innocentReading: Mahindra is a long-standing military vehicle supplier, and the earlier LSV and IADS orders show it was winning MoD work before any bond. The 2025 light-vehicle contract was a Buy (IDDM) award split with Force Motors, which also bought BJP bonds. A 26-month gap between a one-time Rs 25 cr purchase and a split vehicle order is what normal procurement looks like for an incumbent vendor. Donations to the party in power are the commonest pattern among all donors.
verdicts.reason: Each fact in the claim checks out: the IADS award (27 Aug 2021, Rs 1,349.95 cr, Mahindra Defence Systems) and the purchase of 25 x Rs 1 cr BJP bonds on 27 Jan 2023. But the claim's label and the narrative's strongestCounter ("the Mahindra order precedes the bond by 17 months") treat the date test as cutting against a link. The half the claim left unsearched contains a PIB-reported MoD contract dated 27 Mar 2025 signed with Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd itself, the bond-buying entity. That is exactly the claim's own upgradeIf condition, and it is stronger than the condition as written, because the contract is with the parent rather than the subsidiary. The killIf condition did not trigger. As written, the claim selects a pre-bond award and omits a post-bond award to the same legal entity, so it must be rewritten. The tier stays analytic: no record links the bond to the order, and Force Motors, the co-winner, is also a BJP bond buyer, so the order does not discriminate.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Change lab to: "Date test (mixed): two MoD awards to Mahindra Defence Systems precede the 27 Jan 2023 bond (LSV, Mar 2021, Rs 1,056 cr; IADS, 27 Aug 2021, Rs 1,349.95 cr); one MoD contract to Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd follows it (about 1,986 light vehicles, 27 Mar 2025, part of a roughly Rs 700 cr light-vehicle award shared with Force Motors)." (2) Rewrite d to match: delete "Awards after 27 Jan 2023 were not searched" and add the 27 Mar 2025 PIB contract with its source (PIB 27 Mar 2025, mirrored at https://www.devdiscourse.com/article/law-order/3324534-mod-signs-2500-cr-contracts-for-namis-tracked-system-light-vehicles). (3) Rewrite innocentReading to cover the post-bond order: competitive Buy (IDDM) award, co-winner Force Motors also a BJP-only bond buyer, 26-month gap, incumbent supplier. (4) Retire upgradeIf/killIf as written, because the post-bond contract exists. The new upgradeIf should be a full MoD/DAC award list by vendor and date showing bond buyers win at a higher rate than non-buyers such as L&T, Tata Advanced Systems and Bharat Forge. (5) Remove "the Mahindra order precedes the bond by 17 months" from the narrative's strongestCounter, and fix the gap entry that says the test was run for one vendor only. (6) Entity force:mahindra-defence-systems: delete "MoD contracts are with this subsidiary, not with the listed parent". (7) The void entry saying Force Motors' "defence supply line was not established" is wrong: Force Motors won 2,978 LSVs from MoD on 27 Mar 2025. Promote its Rs 6.35 cr of BJP bonds to a bond claim using the same lens.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: the Standing Committee on Defence reported, in a report tabled on 30 Apr 2012 (Antony replied in the Rajya Sabha on 2 May 2012), that the service-conditions period barring officers from private employment was "earlier two years", "now ... reduced to one year". Primary support for the "earlier" half: Pension Regulations for the Army 1961 (Part I), Reg 18(a), which I opened on indianemployees.com, says officers need prior sanction for commercial employment "before the expiry of two years from the date of his/her retirement". A search snippet attributes the one-year version to PRA Part I (2008), Reg 31, but I could not open the PDF: the desw.gov.in certificate has expired and cgda.nic.in returned 503. The change probably came with the 2008 regulations, but no notification date was verified. The edge has from/to = null, so there is no tenure conflict. Nothing found shows the 5-year recommendation was adopted later. The current status as of 2026 has not been checked against a primary source.
verdicts.identityTest: The rule exists, but the target of the edge is too broad. Per PRA 1961 Reg 18(a) and the search-snippet text of the 2008 regulation, it covers only officers "who held the rank of Colonel and above" immediately before retirement who are drawing pension or gratuity. It is not all retired armed forces officers. It is also Army-specific: the Navy and Air Force have their own Pension Regulations, whose texts were not checked. The Standing Committee's 5-year recommendation was for Brigadier and above. The class node force:retired-armed-forces-officers should therefore carry the rank threshold.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not discriminating and implies no wrongdoing. It describes a rule that applies to everyone in the class. The civil-service counterpart, Rule 10 of the CCS (Pension) Rules (force:ccs-pension-rule-10), has the same one-year window for Group A officers. A one-year commercial-employment bar is the norm across Indian central services. Symmetry: the reduction came before or during UPA-II, and the 5-year recommendation was not adopted under UPA-II or, as far as was found, under the NDA. Neither government is singled out.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed because the claim alleges nothing. The government's recorded response, from the Shillong Times on 3 May 2012: Defence Minister A K Antony said "We will examine that recommendation seriously." https://theshillongtimes.com/2012/05/03/govt-to-consider-5-yr-cooling-off-period-for-defence-officers/ . The later PTI report of 15 Sep 2012, reposted on the blog, says a restriction proposal was "prepared and expected to be sent to the armed forces". No adoption was found.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a descriptive statement of the governing rule. Bringing the armed forces in line with the one-year civil-service window (Rule 10) explains the two-to-one change without any inference of capture.
verdicts.reason: The core text holds. The Shillong Times article, quoted verbatim: "The committee noted that the prescribed period as per service conditions forbidding Armed Forces officers joining private sector was earlier two years which has now been reduced to one year". The "earlier two years" half is backed by the primary PRA 1961 Reg 18(a). The claim survives at reported, not documented, for one reason: the one-year figure rests on a press account of a committee report, and I could not open the 2008 regulation itself. However, the field "rule number ... not located" is no longer a bare gap. The 1961 rule is Reg 18(a), and the 2008 rule is reportedly Reg 31. The class is also overstated, since the rule covers only Colonel and above. Both need fixing, but neither refutes the claim.

Label it as such, or replace it with the Business Standard PTI original. 6) Upgrade to documented only after the 2008 PRA Reg 31 text has been opened and quoted.

verdicts.dateTest: Fails as written. The claim reads: Rule 10 of the CCS (Pension) Rules governs retired Group A civil servants (one-year permission window), with no dates (from=null, to=null). The rule's actual windows are as follows. Rule 10 of the 1972 Rules carried the one-year window only from the amendment notified on 23.11.2006. The StaffNews copy of DoPT OM 27012/5/2000-Estt(A) of 5.12.2006 says requests 'received on or after 23.11.2006 shall be governed by the amended provision'. Before that amendment the window was two years. The 1972 Rules were then replaced by the CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 868(E), 20 December 2021). The commercial-employment provision there is Rule 9, not Rule 10. So the edge is accurate only for 23.11.2006 to 19.12.2021. Leaving it undated presents a superseded rule number as current law. The one linked use in the file still holds: the DRDO retiree left service on 2015-01-31 and took the board seat on 2018-01-29, both inside the 1972-Rules period.
verdicts.identityTest: Partly fails. Under the law in force today, 'CCS (Pension) Rule 10' is a different provision: Rule 10 of the 2021 Rules covers 'Employment after retirement under a Government outside India'. The claim text (c024 'text') leaves out '1972', which makes the identity ambiguous. The label 'lab' keeps '1972', so it is right for its period. A second identity problem: the record calls this rule the comparator for 'retired Secretaries'. IAS, IPS and IFoS Secretaries are not covered by the CCS (Pension) Rules. Their equivalent is Rule 26 of the All India Services (DCRB) Rules, 1958. CCS Rule 10/9 covers members of the Central Services, Group A, and holders of Group A posts, such as IRS officers or DRDS scientists. The target class node 'retired Group A civil servants' is broadly right, but the 'd' text overstates what the rule covers.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable as a test of discrimination. This is a rule edge that applies to the whole class (every Central Service Group A retiree), so by design it singles out no one. Symmetry: UPA-I made the one-year amendment in 2006 and the NDA government re-made it as Rule 9 in 2021 with the same one-year window, so the reading is identical across governments. It serves as a neutral comparator for the armed-forces cooling-off rule.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is a statutory instrument, not an accusation, so there is no party to deny it. None found; not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The edge describes a neutral regulatory restriction that serves as a comparator. It implies no wrongdoing. The defect is drafting: an undated, superseded rule number, and a scope wider than the rule (IAS Secretaries fall under AIS DCRB Rule 26). It is not a substantive misstatement of what the rule required between 2006 and 2021.
verdicts.reason: The source holds for the 1972 rule. StaffNews reproduces DoPT OM of 5.12.2006: 'Permission will be required for post retirement commercial employment of a retired officer who was a member of a Group 'A' Central Civil Service or held a Group 'A' post if the commercial employment is to be taken up within one year of retirement.' But the edge is undated and its text says 'CCS (Pension) Rule 10' without '1972'. The CCS (Pension) Rules 2021 (G.S.R. 868(E), 20.12.2021, text on TaxGuru) replaced the 1972 Rules. In the 2021 Rules, Rule 9 now carries the commercial-employment restriction: 'If a pensioner who, immediately before his retirement was a member of Central Service Group 'A' wishes to accept any commercial employment before the expiry of one year from the date of his retirement, he shall obtain the previous sanction of the Government ... in Form 1'. Rule 10 of the 2021 Rules covers employment under a foreign government. So without from/to dates the edge cites the wrong rule as current law. The substance survives once the dates are added and a superseding edge is created. The corrected pair should be tier documented, citing gazette primaries rather than a blog.
verdicts.corrections: 1) c024 text: change to 'CCS (Pension) Rules 1972, Rule 10 (as amended 23.11.2006): permission for commercial employment within one year of retirement (Central Service Group A)'. 2) Set from='2006-11-23' and to='2021-12-19' (the one-year window; before 2006 the window was two years). Set supersededBy to a new edge from a node 'force:ccs-pension-2021-rule-9' (CCS (Pension) Rules 2021, Rule 9, G.S.R. 868(E), 20.12.2021, Form 1) to force:retired-group-a-civil-servants, pred 'law', from='2021-12-20', to=null, tier documented. Source for the new edge: the Gazette/DoPPW text (egazette.gov.in G.S.R. 868(E); TaxGuru reproduction https://taxguru.in/corporate-law/central-civil-services-pension-rules-2021.html). 3) Node force:ccs-pension-rule-10 and the c024 'd': remove 'comparator for retired Secretaries' or qualify it. IAS/IPS/IFoS Secretaries fall under AIS (DCRB) Rules 1958 Rule 26; add that as a separate instrument node if Secretaries are being compared. Also change 'Group A Central Civil Service' to 'Central Service Group A' in line with the 2021 wording. 4) Tier: for documented, add a primary source, either the DoPT OM 27012/5/2000-Estt(A) of 5.12.2006 on persmin.gov.in or the 1972 Rules on the CAG copy (https://cag.gov.in/uploads/media/CCS-Pension-Rules-1972-as-from-DoPT-website-20200717165308.pdf). Otherwise keep reported, since StaffNews is a secondary blog that reproduces the OM. 5) Line 2455 (Astra/DRDO edge): its reliance on 'Rule 10' is valid for the 2015–2018 dates, but it should cite the 1972 Rules explicitly.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: DoPT (Ministry of Personnel) amended CCS (Pension) Rules 1972 Rule 8 by a notification of 31 May 2021. Secondary reproductions of the gazette (staffnews.in Jul 2021, gconnect corrigendum) put it at 31 May 2021, G.S.R. 360(E), Gazette of India Extraordinary Pt II s.3(i). The ORF piece (Harsh V. Pant, 16 Jun 2021) is dated after that, which fits, but it never gives the notification date. It only says "the government gazette notification". So the cited source does not carry the date. Open end (to: null): the 1972 Rules were replaced by the CCS (Pension) Rules 2021 (Dec 2021). The restriction carried over, but the rule number in the consolidated rules should be checked before `to` stays null without a supersede note.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The instrument is the CCS (Pension) Amendment Rules 2021 amending Rule 8 of the 1972 Rules. ORF: "the revision of Rule 8 of the 1972 Act... The rules would cover retired officials of 26 organisations including the Intelligence Bureau, R&AW, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), CBI, NCB, BSF, CRPF, ITBP, and CISF." The governed class (retirees of organisations in the RTI Act Second Schedule) matches the target node. "Not an Army Rules amendment" is correct: CCS (Pension) Rules do not govern armed-forces personnel, who are under the Pension Regulations.
verdicts.baseRate: Not a discriminating-property claim. It is a single statute-to-governed-class edge, so a base rate does not apply. Symmetry control: the provision this amendment widened was a 2007/2008 Rule 8(3)(a) amendment from the UPA-I period, which already required permission (from the head of department) for publishing sensitive information, with pension as the sanction (reported by The Hindu and reproduced at sanjhamorcha.com). The 2021 change widened it to "domain of the organisation", personnel references and expertise, and moved approval to the Head of Organisation. Reading it as UPA vs NDA, both governments restricted publication; NDA widened the scope.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial needed, because the edge states the content of a rule and not wrongdoing. The government's stated purpose (protecting sensitive information under the OSA framework) appears in contemporaneous coverage. I found no DoPT statement disputing the content.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a pension-conditioned confidentiality rule that updates the 2007 provision, aimed at retired intelligence and security staff disclosing organisational information. Comparable to the UK Official Secrets Act 1989 and Australian practice (ORF makes this comparison itself). The edge as written makes no allegation, so it fits this reading.
verdicts.reason: The core claim holds: a CCS (Pension) amendment of 2021 requires retirees of 26 RTI Second Schedule intelligence and security organisations to get prior clearance before publishing, and it is not an Army Rules amendment. The ORF source supports the coverage, the quoted rule text and the Rule 8 revision. It does NOT state the 31 May 2021 date, Rule 8(3)(a), the Form 26 undertaking, or the explicit pension sanction for the new rule. Those details are correct, but they come from the gazette (G.S.R. 360(E), 31 May 2021) as reproduced by staffnews/gconnect, not from the cited source. The claim is not refuted, but the source only partly matches. Tier "reported" is right for the source in hand. Citing the e-gazette G.S.R. 360(E) would justify "documented".
verdicts.corrections: 1) Add the primary source: Gazette of India Extraordinary, G.S.R. 360(E), DoPT notification dated 31 May 2021 (egazette.gov.in), or failing that https://www.staffnews.in/2021/07/central-civil-services-pension-amendment-rules-2021.html. Then upgrade tier to documented. Until then, the date, Rule 8(3)(a) and Form 26 details in `d`/`sub` are not supported by the only cited source. 2) In node force:ccs-pension-amendment-2021 `d[1]` and in c025 `d`: drop "DRI" from the list of officials ORF says were not covered. ORF names DRI among the 26 covered organisations and then muddles it into the non-covered list. Restating that contradiction is an error. Keep "retired armed forces personnel and ED officials". 3) Add the 2007/2008 UPA-era Rule 8(3)(a) predecessor as context or a supersede edge (approval then by Head of Department, with no "domain"/personnel clause) so the change is shown as a widening, not a new restriction. 4) Check `to`/supersededBy against the CCS (Pension) Rules 2021 (Dec 2021), which replaced the 1972 Rules, and record the rule number the provision carries in the consolidated rules.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Avinash Chander held the posts of DG DRDO and Secretary DDR&D from 2013 to 2015-01-31. The sources confirm it. Wikipedia lists him as "In office 2013-2015" and says "on 14 January 2015, the Department of Personnel and Training advised his contract to end ... on 31 January 2015." The Tribune (14 Jan 2015) says he was appointed in May 2013 and "had retired on November 30 last year on attaining the age of 64", that he was kept on by a contract "to end on May 31, 2016", and that the ACC approved ending that contract "with effect from January 31". IBTimes (14 Jan 2015) quotes the ACC order: "approved the termination of the contract of Shri Avinash Chander, Secretary, Department of Defence Research and Development-cum-DG, Defence Research and Development Organisation and Scientific Advisor to Raksha Mantri with effect from 31.01.2015". The Astra Microwave appointment (c027) began on 2018-01-29. That is about 3 years after 2015-01-31, or about 3 years 2 months after his 2014-11-30 superannuation, so the two periods do not overlap. Either date puts the Astra role outside both the one-year window for the armed forces and the one-year window under Rule 10.
verdicts.identityTest: The person is the same. The ACC order names "Shri Avinash Chander, Secretary, Department of Defence Research and Development-cum-DG, DRDO and Scientific Advisor to Raksha Mantri". The Astra AR 2020-21 (c027) describes its director, DIN 05288690, as "the retired Secretary, Defence R&D and Director General, DRDO". He is not the Avinash Chander who was a Lok Sabha / Punjab politician, and Wikipedia gives the scientist his own page. The person also passes the public-rank test: he was Secretary to the Government of India and an ACC appointee.
verdicts.baseRate: The edge only records a tenure and makes no accusation, so no base rate applies to it. The join it enables (a former DRDO head who later sits on the board of a defence vendor) is common for ex-Secretaries and former DRDO lab and cluster heads on defence-electronics boards. That join is therefore weak evidence of anything beyond expertise, and c027 already says so.
verdicts.denialFound: This is not a denial, but it is the recorded response. Chander told IBTimes: "It has come as a shock to me. I haven't received any order from the government ... No idea why it has happened." (https://www.ibtimes.co.in/it-has-come-shock-me-drdo-chief-avinash-chander-termination-his-contract-620286). The government's reason, given by Defence Minister Parrikar, was that the post should not be held by someone on contract and that a younger person should lead DRDO (Business Standard/IANS, 14 Jan 2015). No one disputes the dates.
verdicts.innocentReading: The edge is a plain record of an office and its dates. It has a political background: UPA-II appointed him in May 2013, and the NDA government ended his contract 16 months early. That background is about the removal, not about any wrongdoing tied to the later board seat. Symmetry check: the same edge would read the same way whichever government made the appointment. Wikipedia's phrase "due to poor performance" is not supported by the ACC order or by the press reports, which give Parrikar's stated reason (a younger head who is not on contract). The edge's `d` correctly leaves that phrase out, and it must stay out.
verdicts.reason: The tenure and the end date are confirmed by the ACC order, which the Indian Express and IBTimes quote verbatim, and independently by The Tribune. The end date of 2015-01-31 is correct, and the Astra role (2018-01-29) comes about 3 years later, so the precedence claim holds. The only weakness is the source chain: Wikipedia is the only source cited, and Wikipedia alone is not a credible outlet with named sourcing. With the ACC-order reports added, the edge meets the documented tier (primary order quoted, two independent outlets). The edge's conclusion does not change, but it should note that he superannuated on 2014-11-30 and then served on contract until 2015-01-31.
verdicts.corrections: 1) srcs: keep Wikipedia only as secondary and add The Tribune, 14 Jan 2015 (https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/archive/nation/drdo-chief-told-to-go-before-his-contract-ends-29869) and IBTimes India, 14 Jan 2015, which quotes the ACC order (https://www.ibtimes.co.in/it-has-come-shock-me-drdo-chief-avinash-chander-termination-his-contract-620286). Then set the tier to documented. If those sources are not added, keep reported. 2) from: change "2013" to "2013-05" (appointed May 2013; first of June 2013 per press, so verify the exact day before writing it). 3) d: add "superannuated 2014-11-30 at 64, then continued on contract (originally to 2016-05-31); ACC terminated the contract w.e.f. 31.01.2015." State that the cooling-off gap is about 3 years from 2015-01-31, or about 3 years 2 months from 2014-11-30, and that both dates fall outside every one-year window. 4) Do not import Wikipedia's "poor performance" wording. If a reason is given, cite Parrikar's stated reason (younger head, no contract appointment) alongside Chander's "shock / no idea why" response. 5) The force:drdo node `d` carries the same Wikipedia-only cite and should get the same source fix.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: Fali Homi Major held the post of Chief of the Air Staff, IAF, from 2007-03-31 to 2009-05-31. The Wikipedia infobox gives the same dates: in office "31 March 2007" to "31 May 2009", preceded by S. P. Tyagi and succeeded by P. V. Naik. The primary record agrees on the start date. verdicts.identityTest: The node per:fali-major is Fali Homi Major, 21st CAS, service number 11442 GD(P), born 29 May 1947 (PIB). This is the same person the Wikipedia, PIB and Bharat Rakshak records describe. The target force:indian-air-force is correct. No namesake ambiguity.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable. This is a plain date-ranged role edge with no implied property or wrongdoing. Every service chief has such an edge. It is only useful as an input to the cooling-off test.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim is neutral biographical fact with nothing to deny. None found, not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The claim is itself the innocent reading: a public office held for fixed dates. It carries no imputation. The `d` note correctly records the retirement date for the cooling-off test. His Reliance Defence board role (2016) came about 7 years after retirement, so the edge does not engage cooling-off by itself.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives. Every date, the office, the predecessor and the successor match Wikipedia, the Bharat Rakshak service record and the primary PIB/MoD release of 31 March 2007, which states Major took over from Tyagi "today". He is a service chief at public rank and the edge has no operational detail. A primary government release confirms the start date, so the edge can move up to documented if the PIB source is added. If only the Wikipedia source stays, keep it at reported.
verdicts.corrections: Add srcs ["PIB (MoD) 31-Mar-2007 — Air Chief Marshal FH Major takes over as the Chief of Air Staff", "https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/erelcontent.aspx?relid=26545"] and ["Bharat Rakshak — Service record 11442 GD(P)", "https://www.bharat-rakshak.com/indianairforce/database/11442"].
